title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: For two days after that, Rostov didn't see Dolokhov — either at his own home or at Dolokhov's. On the third day, he received a note from him:

Since I don't intend to visit your home again for reasons you are aware of, and since I'm leaving to rejoin my regiment, I'm giving a farewell supper tonight for my friends. Come to the English Hotel.

Around ten o'clock, Rostov went to the English Hotel straight from the theater, where he'd been with his family and Denisov. He was immediately shown to the best room, which Dolokhov had reserved for the evening. About twenty men were gathered around a table where Dolokhov sat between two candles. On the table was a pile of gold coins and paper money — he was running the bank. Rostov hadn't seen him since the proposal and Sonya's refusal, and he felt uneasy at the thought of how they would meet.
Dolokhov's clear, cold gaze met Rostov the moment he walked through the door, as though he'd been waiting for him a long time.
"It's been a while since we've seen each other," he said. "Thanks for coming. I'll just finish dealing, and then Ilyushka will come with his singers."
"I stopped by your place once or twice," said Rostov, blushing.
Dolokhov said nothing in reply.
"You can play if you like," he said.
Rostov remembered a strange conversation he'd once had with Dolokhov. "Only fools trust to luck in cards," Dolokhov had said then.
"Or are you afraid to play with me?" Dolokhov asked now, as if reading Rostov's thoughts.

Beneath Dolokhov's smile, Rostov recognized the mood he'd seen at the club dinner and on other occasions — when Dolokhov, as if tired of everyday life, felt driven to break free of it through some wild and usually cruel action.

Rostov felt uneasy. He tried and failed to come up with some joke to deflect Dolokhov's words. But before he could think of anything, Dolokhov looked him straight in the face and said slowly and deliberately, loud enough for everyone to hear:
"Remember our conversation about cards? 'Only a fool trusts to luck — you should make certain.' Well, I want to put that to the test."
"Test his luck, or his certainty?" Rostov wondered to himself.
"Well, you'd better not play then," Dolokhov added, and cracking open a new pack of cards, he announced: "Bank, gentlemen!"
He pushed the money forward and began dealing. Rostov sat down beside him but didn't play at first. Dolokhov kept glancing at him.
"Why aren't you playing?" he asked.
And strangely, Nicholas felt he couldn't help himself — he picked up a card, placed a small bet on it, and began to play.
"I don't have any money on me," he said.
"I'll trust you."
Rostov bet five rubles on a card and lost. He bet again and lost again. Dolokhov "killed" — that is, beat — ten of Rostov's cards in a row.
"Gentlemen," said Dolokhov after dealing for some time, "please put your money on the cards, or I'll get confused with the accounts."
One of the players said he hoped he could be trusted.
"Of course you can, but I'm afraid of mixing up the numbers. So please put the money on your cards," Dolokhov replied. "Don't hold back — we'll settle up later," he added, turning to Rostov.
The game continued. A waiter kept circulating with champagne.

Rostov kept losing. He had eight hundred rubles marked against him. He wrote "800 rubles" on a card, but while the waiter filled his glass, he changed his mind and crossed it out to write his usual stake of twenty rubles.
"Leave it," said Dolokhov, though he didn't seem to even be looking at Rostov. "You'll win it back faster that way. I lose to the others but win from you. Or are you afraid of me?" he asked again.

Rostov gave in. He left the eight hundred and laid down a seven of hearts with a torn corner that he'd picked up from the floor. He would remember that seven for a long time afterward. He set down the seven of hearts, on which he'd written "800 rubles" in clear upright figures with a broken piece of chalk. He drained the glass of warm champagne that was handed to him, smiled at Dolokhov's words, and with a sinking heart, waiting for a seven to come up, watched Dolokhov's hands holding the deck. A great deal depended on whether Rostov won or lost on that seven of hearts. The previous Sunday, the old count had given his son two thousand rubles and, though he always hated discussing money problems, had told Nicholas that this was all he could give him until May, and asked him to be more careful this time. Nicholas had replied that it would be more than enough and had given his word of honor not to ask for anything more until spring. Now only twelve hundred rubles remained, so this seven of hearts meant not just the loss of sixteen hundred rubles, but the shame of breaking his word. With a sinking heart he watched Dolokhov's hands and thought, "Come on, hurry up and give me this card, and I'll grab my hat and drive home to supper with Denisov, Natasha, and Sonya, and I swear I'll never touch a card again." At that moment, his home life — the jokes with Petya, the conversations with Sonya, the duets with Natasha, the card games with his father, even his comfortable bed in the house on the Povarskaya — rose before him with such vividness and warmth that it felt like a lost, unappreciated paradise. He couldn't grasp that a stupid twist of chance — the seven landing to the right instead of the left — could strip him of all this happiness, which he was only now truly appreciating, and plunge him into some unknown abyss of misery. It couldn't be — and yet he waited with a sinking heart for the movement of Dolokhov's hands. Those broad, reddish hands with their hairy wrists showing below the shirt cuffs set down the deck and picked up a glass and pipe that were offered to him.
"So you're not afraid to play with me?" Dolokhov repeated, and as if about to tell a good story, he put down the cards, leaned back in his chair, and began deliberately, with a smile:
"Yes, gentlemen, I've heard there's a rumor going around Moscow that I'm a cheat, so I advise you all to be careful."
"Come on, deal!" Rostov burst out.
"Oh, those Moscow gossips!" said Dolokhov, and he picked up the cards with a smile.
"Aah!" Rostov nearly screamed, clutching his head with both hands. The seven he needed was lying on top — the first card in the deck. He had lost more than he could ever pay.
"Still, don't ruin yourself," said Dolokhov with a sidelong glance at Rostov as he continued dealing.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: An hour and a half later, most of the players had lost interest in their own games.

All attention was now focused on Rostov. Instead of sixteen hundred rubles, he had a long column of figures scored against him — he'd calculated it at around ten thousand, but it must have been closer to fifteen thousand by now, he vaguely thought. In reality, it had already passed twenty thousand rubles. Dolokhov had stopped listening to stories or telling them. He followed every movement of Rostov's hands and occasionally glanced at the running total of his debt. He had decided to keep playing until the score reached forty-three thousand. He'd chosen that number because forty-three was the sum of his own age and Sonya's. Rostov, his head propped on both hands, sat at the table, which was covered in scrawled figures, stained with spilled wine, and littered with cards. One agonizing thought wouldn't leave him: that those broad-boned, reddish hands with hairy wrists showing below the shirt sleeves — those hands he both loved and hated — held him completely in their power.

"Six hundred rubles, ace, a corner, a nine... winning it back is impossible... Oh, how good it was at home!... The jack, double or nothing... it can't be!... And why is he doing this to me?" Rostov's thoughts raced. Sometimes he staked a large sum, but Dolokhov refused to accept it and set the stake himself. Nicholas submitted, and one moment he was praying to God — as he had on the battlefield at the bridge over the Enns — and the next he was guessing that whichever card he happened to pull first from the crumpled pile under the table would save him. Then he counted the braids on his coat and bet on a card with that number, or tried to stake the full total of his losses on a single card. Then he looked around for help from the other players, or peered at Dolokhov's cold, impassive face, trying to read what was going on behind it.

"He must know what this loss means to me. He can't want to ruin me. Wasn't he my friend? Didn't I care about him? But it's not his fault — what can he do if luck runs his way?... And it's not my fault either," he told himself. "I haven't done anything wrong. Have I killed anyone? Have I insulted anyone or wished anyone harm? Then why this terrible disaster? And when did it start? Just a little while ago, I sat down at this table planning to win a hundred rubles to buy a box for Mama's name day and then go home. I was so happy, so free, so carefree! I didn't even realize how happy I was! When did that end, and when did this new, awful reality begin? What was the turning point? I've been sitting in the same place at this same table the whole time, choosing cards and placing bets, watching those same broad-boned, agile hands. When did it happen? What happened? I'm healthy and strong, still the same person in the same place. No — it can't be! Surely it will all turn out to be nothing!"
He was flushed and drenched in sweat, though the room wasn't warm. His face was terrible and pitiful to see, especially because of his helpless efforts to appear calm.

The score against him reached the fateful sum of forty-three thousand. Rostov had just prepared a card — planning to bend the corner to double the three thousand just added to his debt — when Dolokhov slammed the deck down, pushed it aside, and began rapidly tallying Rostov's total, the chalk snapping as he marked the figures in his clear, bold handwriting.
"Supper — it's time for supper! And here are the gypsies!"
A group of dark-skinned men and women were indeed coming in from the cold, saying something in their Romani accents. Nicholas understood it was all over, but he said in a casual tone:
"Well, aren't we going to continue? I had a wonderful card ready" — as if the fun of the game were all he cared about.
"It's finished! I'm ruined!" he thought. "A bullet through my brain — that's all that's left!" And at the same time, he said cheerfully:
"Come on, just one more little card!"

"All right," said Dolokhov, having finished adding up the figures. "All right — twenty-one rubles," he said, pointing to the number twenty-one that pushed the total just past the round sum of forty-three thousand. He picked up a new deck and prepared to deal. Rostov obediently straightened the bent corner of his card and, instead of the six thousand he'd planned to bet, carefully wrote "twenty-one."
"It doesn't matter to me," he said. "I just want to see whether you'll let me win this ten or beat it."
Dolokhov began dealing in earnest. Oh, how Rostov loathed those hands at that moment — those short, reddish fingers with their hairy wrists that held him in their power... The ten went to Dolokhov.
"You owe forty-three thousand, Count," said Dolokhov, and stretching, he rose from the table. "Sitting so long really does tire you out," he added.
"Yes, I'm tired too," said Rostov.
Dolokhov cut him short, as if to remind him that this was no time for casual remarks.
"When can I expect the money, Count?"
Rostov, flushing, drew Dolokhov into the next room.
"I can't pay it all at once. Will you accept a promissory note?" he said.
"Listen, Rostov," said Dolokhov clearly, smiling and looking Nicholas straight in the eyes. "You know the saying — 'Lucky in love, unlucky at cards.' Your cousin is in love with you. I know."

"Oh, how terrible to feel so completely in this man's power," thought Rostov. He knew the shock this loss would inflict on his father and mother. He knew what a relief it would be to escape it all. And he felt that Dolokhov knew he could save him from all this shame and misery — but chose instead to toy with him, the way a cat plays with a mouse.
"Your cousin..." Dolokhov began, but Nicholas interrupted him.
"My cousin has nothing to do with this, and there's no need to bring her into it!" he burst out fiercely.
"Then when will I have the money?"
"Tomorrow," Rostov replied, and left the room.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Saying "tomorrow" and keeping up a dignified front wasn't difficult. But going home alone, facing his sisters, brother, mother, and father, confessing what he'd done, and asking for money he had no right to after giving his word of honor — that was terrible.

At home, they hadn't gone to bed yet. The young people had come back from the theater, had supper, and were gathered around the clavichord. The moment Nicholas walked in, he was enveloped by the romantic atmosphere that had pervaded the Rostov household all winter — and which, after Dolokhov's proposal and Iogel's ball, seemed to have grown even thicker around Sonya and Natasha, like the air before a thunderstorm. Sonya and Natasha were standing by the clavichord in the light blue dresses they'd worn to the theater, looking pretty and aware of it, happy and smiling. Vera was playing chess with Shinshin in the drawing room. The old countess, waiting for her husband and son to come home, was playing patience with the elderly gentlewoman who lived with the family. Denisov, his eyes sparkling and his hair disheveled, sat at the clavichord striking chords with his short fingers, his legs thrown back and his eyes rolling as he sang in his small, husky, but true voice some verses he'd composed called "Enchantress," for which he was trying to find the right music:
Enchantress, say, to my forsaken lyre / What magic power is this recalls me still? / What spark has set my inmost soul on fire, / What is this bliss that makes my fingers thrill?
He sang with passion, his sparkling dark eyes fixed on the frightened and happy Natasha.
"Wonderful! Brilliant!" exclaimed Natasha. "Another verse!" she said, without even noticing Nicholas.
"Everything's the same with them," thought Nicholas, glancing into the drawing room where he saw Vera and his mother with the old lady.
"Oh, Nicholas is here!" cried Natasha, running up to him.
"Is Papa home?" he asked.
"I'm so glad you've come!" said Natasha, ignoring his question. "We're having such a wonderful time! Vasili Dmitrich is staying an extra day just for me! Did you know?"
"No, Papa isn't back yet," said Sonya.
"Nicholas, is that you? Come here, darling!" called the old countess from the drawing room.
Nicholas went to her, kissed her hand, and sat down silently at her table, watching her hands arrange the cards. From the music room came laughter and cheerful voices urging Natasha to sing.
"All wight! All wight!" Denisov shouted. "No more excuses! It's your turn to sing the ba'cawolla — I beg you!"
The countess glanced at her silent son.
"What's wrong?" she asked.
"Oh, nothing," he said, as though tired of being asked the same question over and over. "Will Papa be home soon?"
"I think so."
"Everything's the same with them. They know nothing about it! Where can I go?" Nicholas thought, and he went back to the music room where the clavichord stood.
Sonya was at the clavichord, playing the prelude to Denisov's favorite barcarolle. Natasha was getting ready to sing. Denisov was watching her with adoring eyes.
Nicholas began pacing up and down the room.
"Why do they want her to sing? How can she sing? There's nothing to be happy about!" he thought.
Sonya struck the first chord of the prelude.
"My God, I'm a ruined and disgraced man! A bullet through my brain is the only thing left for me — not singing!" his thoughts ran on. "Leave? But where? It doesn't matter — let them sing!"
He continued pacing the room, looking darkly at Denisov and the girls, avoiding their eyes.
"Nikolenka, what's wrong?" Sonya's eyes seemed to ask. She noticed at once that something had happened to him.

Nicholas turned away from her. Natasha too, with her quick instincts, had instantly noticed her brother's state. But though she saw it, she was so full of joy at that moment, so far from any sorrow, sadness, or self-reproach, that she deliberately fooled herself, as young people often do. "No, I'm too happy right now to let anyone's suffering spoil it," she felt, and told herself: "No, I must be wrong — he's probably just as happy as I am."
"Ready, Sonya!" she said, walking to the very center of the room, where she believed the acoustics were best.
She lifted her head, let her arms drop limply at her sides like a ballet dancer, and, rising energetically from her heels to her toes, stepped to the middle of the room and stood still.
"Yes, this is me!" she seemed to say, responding to the rapt gaze with which Denisov followed her.
"And what is she so pleased about?" Nicholas thought, looking at his sister. "Why doesn't she feel gloomy and ashamed?"

Natasha took her first note. Her throat swelled, her chest rose, her eyes grew serious. In that moment she was oblivious to everything around her, and from her smiling lips flowed sounds that anyone can produce at the same intervals and sustain for the same duration — but which leave you cold a thousand times, and on the thousand-and-first time make you tremble and weep.

That winter, Natasha had begun singing seriously for the first time, mainly because Denisov took such delight in her voice. She no longer sang like a child — the comical, painstaking, childish quality was gone. But she didn't yet sing well, as every expert who heard her would say: "It's an untrained voice, but a beautiful one that needs proper training." Except they usually said this some time after she'd finished. While that untrained voice was actually sounding — with its imperfect breathing and labored transitions — even the critics said nothing. They simply listened with pleasure and wanted to hear more. In her voice there was a virginal freshness, an unawareness of her own gifts, and a velvety softness that had not yet been shaped by art — and these qualities blended so perfectly with her lack of technique that it seemed nothing about that voice could be changed without ruining it.

"What is this?" thought Nicholas, listening with wide eyes. "What's happened to her? How she's singing today!" And suddenly the whole world narrowed for him to the anticipation of the next note, the next phrase, and everything divided into three beats: "Oh mio crudele affetto"... One, two, three... one, two, three... One... "Oh mio crudele affetto"... One, two, three... One. "Oh, this senseless life of ours!" thought Nicholas. "All this misery, and money, and Dolokhov, and anger, and honor — it's all nonsense... but this is real... Come on, Natasha, come on, darling! Come on, sweetheart! How will she take that high note? She took it! Thank God!" And without realizing he was singing, he added a harmony — a second and then a third below the high note. "Oh God, how beautiful! Did I really hit that note? How wonderful!" he thought.

Oh, how that chord vibrated, and how deeply it stirred the finest part of Rostov's soul! And this was something apart from everything else in the world, something above everything in the world. "What are losses, and Dolokhov, and words of honor?... All nonsense! A person could kill and rob and still be happy..."

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: It had been a long time since Rostov had enjoyed music as much as he did that day. But the moment Natasha finished her barcarolle, reality came crashing back. He got up without a word and went downstairs to his own room. Fifteen minutes later the old count came home from his club, cheerful and pleased with himself. Nicholas, hearing the carriage pull up, went to meet him.
"Well — did you have a good time?" said the old count, beaming proudly at his son.
Nicholas tried to say "Yes," but could barely get the word out — he nearly burst into sobs. The count was lighting his pipe and didn't notice his son's state.

"It can't be helped!" thought Nicholas, for the first and last time. And suddenly, in the most casual tone he could manage — a tone that made him ashamed of himself — he said, as if merely asking his father for the carriage to go into town:
"Papa, I've come about a matter of business. I nearly forgot. I need some money."
"Oh dear!" said his father, who was in an especially good mood. "I told you it wouldn't be enough. How much?"

"Quite a lot," said Nicholas, flushing, and with a stupid, careless smile for which he could never forgive himself afterward. "I've lost a little — I mean a good deal, a great deal — forty-three thousand."
"What! To whom? Nonsense!" cried the count, suddenly reddening with a rush of blood to his neck and the back of his head, the way old men do.
"I promised to pay tomorrow," said Nicholas.
"Well!" said the old count, spreading out his arms and sinking helplessly onto the sofa.

"It can't be helped! It happens to everyone!" said the son in a bold, offhand tone, while deep in his soul he saw himself as a worthless scoundrel whose entire life couldn't make up for his crime. He longed to kiss his father's hands and beg forgiveness on his knees, yet he spoke in a careless, even rude voice, saying that it happens to everyone!
The old count dropped his eyes at his son's words and began frantically searching around for something.
"Yes, yes," he muttered, "it'll be hard, I'm afraid — hard to raise... happens to everybody! Yes, who hasn't done it?"
And with a furtive glance at his son's face, the count left the room. Nicholas had been prepared for resistance, but had not at all expected this.
"Papa! Papa!" he called after him, sobbing. "Forgive me!" And seizing his father's hand, he pressed it to his lips and burst into tears.
While father and son were having this conversation, the mother and daughter were having one no less important. Natasha came running to her mother, breathless with excitement.
"Mama! Mama! He's made me..."
"Made what?"
"Made me — he's proposed, Mama! Mama!" she exclaimed.
The countess couldn't believe her ears. Denisov had proposed. To whom? To this slip of a girl, Natasha, who not long ago was playing with dolls and was still having lessons.
"Don't be silly, Natasha! What nonsense!" she said, hoping it was a joke.
"Nonsense indeed! I'm telling you it's true," said Natasha indignantly. "I've come to ask you what to do, and you call it 'nonsense!'"
The countess shrugged her shoulders.
"If it's true that Monsieur Denisov has proposed to you, tell him he's a fool — that's all!"
"No, he's not a fool!" replied Natasha, indignant and serious.
"Well then, what do you want? You're all in love these days. Fine — if you're in love, marry him!" said the countess with an annoyed laugh. "Good luck to you!"
"No, Mama, I'm not in love with him. I don't think I'm in love with him."
"Well then, tell him so."
"Mama, are you angry? Don't be angry, darling! Is it my fault?"
"No, but what is all this, my dear? Do you want me to go tell him?" said the countess with a smile.

"No, I'll do it myself — just tell me what to say. It's easy for you," said Natasha, smiling back. "You should have seen how he said it! I know he didn't mean to say it — it just slipped out accidentally."
"Well, all the same, you must refuse him."
"No, I can't. I feel so sorry for him! He's so nice."
"Well then, accept his proposal. It's high time you were married," the countess answered sharply and sarcastically.
"No, Mama, but I feel so sorry for him. I don't know how to say it."
"And there's nothing for you to say. I'll speak to him myself," said the countess, indignant that anyone should dare treat this little Natasha as a grown-up.

"No, absolutely not! I'll tell him myself, and you can listen at the door," and Natasha ran through the drawing room to the ballroom, where Denisov sat on the same chair by the clavichord with his face in his hands.
He jumped up at the sound of her light step.
"Nataly," he said, rushing toward her with quick steps, "decide my fate. It is in your hands."
"Vasili Dmitrich, I feel so sorry for you! No, but you are so nice... but it won't do... not that... but as a friend, I will always love you."

Denisov bent over her hand, and she heard strange sounds she didn't understand. She kissed his rough, curly black head. At that instant they heard the quick rustle of the countess's dress. She came up to them.

"Vasili Dmitrich, I thank you for the honor," she said in an embarrassed voice that sounded severe to Denisov, "but my daughter is so young, and I would have thought that, as my son's friend, you would have spoken to me first. In that case you would not have forced me to give this refusal."
"Countess..." said Denisov, with downcast eyes and a guilty expression. He tried to say more but faltered.
Natasha could not bear seeing him in such distress. She began to sob aloud.

"Countess, I was wrong," Denisov continued in an unsteady voice, "but believe me, I adore your daughter and all your family so much that I would give my life twice over..." He looked at the countess, and seeing her stern face said: "Well, goodbye, Countess," and kissing her hand, he strode out of the room without looking at Natasha.

The next day Rostov saw Denisov off. He didn't want to stay another day in Moscow. All of Denisov's Moscow friends gave him a farewell party at the gypsies', with the result that he had no memory of how he was put in the sleigh or of the first three stages of his journey.

After Denisov's departure, Rostov spent another two weeks in Moscow without leaving the house, waiting for the money his father couldn't raise right away, and he spent most of his time in the girls' room.

Sonya was more tender and devoted to him than ever. It was as if she wanted to show him that his losses were something noble that made her love him all the more, but Nicholas now considered himself unworthy of her.

He filled the girls' albums with verses and music, and having at last sent Dolokhov the full forty-three thousand rubles and received his receipt, he left at the end of November — without taking leave of any of his acquaintances — to rejoin his regiment, which was already in Poland.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: After his confrontation with his wife, Pierre left for Petersburg. At the Torzhok post station, either there were no horses or the postmaster refused to provide them. Pierre was forced to wait. Without undressing, he lay down on the leather sofa in front of a round table, put his big feet in their heavy boots up on the table, and began to think.
"Shall I bring in the bags? Get a bed ready? Some tea?" asked his valet.

Pierre didn't answer — he neither heard nor saw anything. He had started thinking at the last station and was still turning over the same question — one so important that he noticed nothing around him. Not only did it not matter whether he reached Petersburg sooner or later, or whether he found a room at this station, but compared to the thoughts consuming him it was all the same whether he stayed there a few hours or the rest of his life.

The postmaster, his wife, the valet, and a peasant woman selling Torzhok embroidery came into the room offering their services. Without changing his careless posture, Pierre looked at them over his spectacles, unable to understand what they wanted or how they could go on living without having solved the problems that absorbed him. He had been gripped by these same thoughts ever since the day he returned from Sokolniki after the duel and spent that first agonizing, sleepless night. But now, in the solitude of the journey, they seized him with special force. No matter what he thought about, he always came back to these same questions he could not solve yet could not stop asking himself. It was as if the thread of the main screw holding his life together had been stripped, so that the screw could neither go in nor come out, but just kept turning uselessly in the same place.

The postmaster came in and began obsequiously begging his excellency to wait only two hours, when — come what may — he would provide the courier horses. It was obvious he was lying and only wanted to squeeze more money out of the traveler.

"Is this good or bad?" Pierre asked himself. "It's good for me, bad for another traveler, and unavoidable for himself, because he needs money for food. The man told me that an officer once beat him for letting a private traveler have the courier horses. But the officer beat him because he needed to get somewhere quickly. And I," Pierre continued, "I shot Dolokhov because I felt insulted, and Louis XVI was executed because they considered him a criminal, and a year later they executed those who executed him — also for some reason. What is bad? What is good? What should one love, and what should one hate? What does one live for? And what am I? What is life, and what is death? What power governs everything?"

There was no answer to any of these questions, except one — and that was not a logical answer, not really a reply at all. The answer was: "You'll die and everything will end. You'll die and either learn everything or stop asking." But dying was terrifying too.

The Torzhok peddler woman, in a whining voice, kept offering her goods, especially a pair of goatskin slippers. "I have hundreds of rubles I don't know what to do with, and she stands there in her tattered coat, looking timidly at me," he thought. "And what does she want the money for? As if money could add even a fraction to happiness or peace of mind. Can anything in the world make her or me less vulnerable to evil and death? — death, which ends everything and must come today or tomorrow — in any case, in an instant compared to eternity." And again he twisted the stripped screw, and again it turned uselessly in the same place.

His servant handed him a half-finished epistolary novel by Madame de Souza. He began reading about the sufferings and virtuous struggles of a certain Emilie de Mansfeld. "And why did she resist her seducer when she loved him?" he thought. "God could not have placed in her heart a desire that went against His will. My wife — as she once was — did not resist, and perhaps she was right. Nothing has been found out, nothing has been discovered," Pierre told himself again. "All we can know is that we know nothing. And that's the height of human wisdom."
Everything within and around him seemed confused, senseless, and repulsive. Yet in this very disgust with all his circumstances, Pierre found a kind of bitter satisfaction.
"I must ask your excellency to move over a bit for this gentleman," said the postmaster, entering the room followed by another traveler, also stranded for lack of horses.
The newcomer was a short, large-boned, yellow-faced, wrinkled old man with bushy gray eyebrows hanging over bright eyes of an indefinite grayish color.

Pierre took his feet off the table, stood up, and lay down on a bed that had been prepared for him, glancing now and then at the newcomer. The old man, with a gloomy, tired expression, was wearily removing his wraps with his servant's help, not looking at Pierre. Wearing felt boots on his thin bony legs and keeping on his worn, nankeen-covered sheepskin coat, the traveler sat down on the sofa, leaned back his large head with its broad temples and close-cropped hair, and looked at Bezukhov. The stern, shrewd, penetrating expression of that gaze struck Pierre. He felt a desire to speak to the stranger, but by the time he had made up his mind to ask about the roads, the traveler had closed his eyes. His shriveled old hands were folded, and on one finger Pierre noticed a large cast-iron ring with a seal depicting a death's head. The stranger sat motionless, either resting or — as it seemed to Pierre — sunk in profound, calm meditation. His servant was also a yellow, wrinkled old man, without a beard or mustache — not because he was shaven but because they had never grown. This lively old servant was unpacking the traveler's canteen and preparing tea. He brought in a boiling samovar. When everything was ready, the stranger opened his eyes, moved to the table, and poured a glass of tea for himself and one for the beardless old man, to whom he passed it. Pierre began to feel a growing uneasiness and a sense that it was somehow necessary — even inevitable — to speak with this stranger.
The servant brought back his glass turned upside down, with an unfinished piece of nibbled sugar, and asked if anything else was needed.
* To indicate he didn't want more tea.
"No. Give me the book," said the stranger.

The servant handed him a book that Pierre took to be a devotional work, and the traveler became absorbed in it. Pierre watched him. Suddenly the stranger closed the book, put in a marker, and again leaned back on the sofa in his former position with his eyes shut. Pierre looked at him but didn't have time to look away before the old man opened his eyes and fixed his steady, severe gaze directly on Pierre's face.
Pierre felt flustered and wanted to avoid that look, but the bright old eyes drew him in irresistibly.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: "I have the pleasure of addressing Count Bezukhov, if I'm not mistaken," said the stranger in a deliberate, loud voice.
Pierre looked at him silently and questioningly over his spectacles.

"I have heard of you, my dear sir," the stranger continued, "and of your misfortune." He seemed to emphasize the last word, as if to say: "Yes, misfortune! Call it what you like, I know that what happened to you in Moscow was a misfortune." "I am very sorry, my dear sir."
Pierre flushed and, hurriedly swinging his legs off the bed, leaned toward the old man with a forced, timid smile.
"I haven't brought this up out of curiosity, my dear sir, but for more important reasons."

He paused, his gaze still fixed on Pierre, and moved aside on the sofa as if inviting him to sit down. Pierre felt reluctant to start a conversation with this old man, but found himself involuntarily drawn to him, and sat down beside him.
"You are unhappy, my dear sir," the stranger continued. "You are young and I am old. I would like to help you as far as I can."
"Oh, yes!" said Pierre, with a forced smile. "I'm very grateful to you. Where are you traveling from?"
The stranger's face was not warm — it was even cold and stern — but despite this, both his face and his words were irresistibly compelling to Pierre.
"But if for any reason you don't feel like talking to me," said the old man, "just say so, my dear sir." And he suddenly smiled, in an unexpectedly tender, fatherly way.
"Oh no, not at all! On the contrary, I'm very glad to meet you," said Pierre. And glancing at the stranger's hands again, he looked more closely at the ring with its skull — a Masonic sign.
"May I ask," he said, "are you a Mason?"
"Yes, I belong to the Brotherhood of the Freemasons," said the stranger, looking deeper and deeper into Pierre's eyes. "And in their name and my own, I extend to you a brotherly hand."

"I'm afraid," said Pierre, smiling, torn between the trust this Freemason inspired in him and his old habit of mocking Masonic beliefs, "I'm afraid I'm very far from understanding — how should I put it? — I'm afraid my way of seeing the world is so opposed to yours that we won't understand one another."

"I know your outlook," said the Mason, "and the view of life you mention, which you think is the product of your own thinking, is actually the view held by the majority of people. It is the predictable result of pride, laziness, and ignorance. Forgive me, my dear sir, but if I hadn't known that, I would not have spoken to you. Your view of life is a regrettable delusion."
"Just as I might suppose you to be deluded," said Pierre with a faint smile.

"I would never dare claim to know the truth," said the Mason, whose words struck Pierre more and more with their precision and conviction. "No one can reach the truth alone. Only by laying stone on stone, with the cooperation of all — through millions of generations from our forefather Adam to our own time — is that temple built which will be a worthy dwelling place of the Great God," he added, and closed his eyes.
"I should tell you that I don't believe — don't believe in God," said Pierre regretfully and with effort, feeling it was essential to speak the whole truth.

The Mason looked intently at Pierre and smiled, the way a rich man with millions might smile at a poor fellow who told him that he, the poor man, didn't have the five rubles that would make him happy.
"Yes, you do not know Him, my dear sir," said the Mason. "You cannot know Him. You do not know Him, and that is why you are unhappy."
"Yes, yes, I am unhappy," Pierre agreed. "But what am I to do?"

"You do not know Him, my dear sir, and so you are deeply unhappy. You do not know Him, but He is here — He is in me, He is in my words, He is in you, and even in those blasphemous words you have just spoken!" the Mason pronounced in a stern, trembling voice.
He paused and sighed, evidently trying to calm himself.

"If He did not exist," he said quietly, "you and I would not be speaking of Him, my dear sir. Of what, of whom, are we speaking? Whom have you denied?" he suddenly asked with commanding authority in his voice. "Who invented Him, if He did not exist? Where did your very idea of such an incomprehensible Being come from — a Being all-powerful, eternal, and infinite in all His attributes?"
He fell silent and remained quiet for a long time.
Pierre could not and did not wish to break this silence.

"He exists, but understanding Him is hard," the Mason began again, looking not at Pierre but straight ahead, and turning the pages of his book with old hands that he could not keep still from emotion. "If He were a man whose existence you doubted, I could bring him to you — I could take him by the hand and show him to you. But how can I, an insignificant mortal, show His omnipotence, His infinity, and all His mercy to one who is blind, or who shuts his eyes so as not to see or understand Him, and not to see or understand his own wretchedness and sinfulness?" He paused again. "Who are you? You imagine you are wise because you could utter those blasphemous words," he went on, with a somber, scornful smile. "And you are more foolish and unreasonable than a small child who, playing with the parts of a skillfully made watch, dares to say that since he doesn't understand its purpose, he doesn't believe in the maker who created it. To know Him is hard. For ages, from our forefather Adam to our own day, we have labored to attain that knowledge and are still infinitely far from our goal; but in our lack of understanding we see only our weakness and His greatness."

Pierre listened with a swelling heart, gazing into the Mason's face with shining eyes, not interrupting or questioning him, but believing with his whole soul everything the stranger said. Whether he accepted the wise reasoning in the Mason's words, or believed as a child believes — in the speaker's tone of conviction and earnestness, in the tremor of his voice that sometimes nearly broke, in those brilliant aged eyes grown old in this conviction, in the calm certainty of his calling that radiated from his whole being (and which struck Pierre especially by contrast with his own dejection and hopelessness) — at any rate, Pierre longed with his whole soul to believe, and he did believe, and felt a joyful sense of comfort, renewal, and return to life.
"He is not grasped by reason, but by life," said the Mason.

"I don't understand," said Pierre, feeling with dismay that doubts were reawakening. He was afraid of any lack of clarity, any weakness, in the Mason's arguments; he feared losing the ability to believe in him. "I don't understand," he said, "how it is that the human mind cannot attain the knowledge of which you speak."
The Mason smiled his gentle, fatherly smile.

"The highest wisdom and truth are like the purest liquid we might wish to drink," he said. "Can I receive that pure liquid in a dirty vessel and judge its purity? Only through the inner purification of myself can I keep the liquid I receive in any degree of purity."
"Yes, yes, that's right," said Pierre joyfully.

"The highest wisdom is not founded on reason alone — not on those worldly sciences like physics, history, and chemistry into which intellectual knowledge is divided. The highest wisdom is one. The highest wisdom has only one science — the science of the whole, the science that explains all of creation and man's place in it. To receive that science, it is necessary to purify and renew one's inner self, and so before one can know, it is necessary to believe and to perfect oneself. To that end, we have the light called conscience, which God has implanted in our souls."
"Yes, yes," Pierre agreed.

"Look at your inner self with the eyes of the spirit, and ask yourself whether you are content with yourself. What have you achieved by relying on reason alone? What are you? You are young, you are rich, you are clever, you are well educated. And what have you done with all these gifts? Are you satisfied with yourself and your life?"
"No, I hate my life," Pierre muttered, wincing.

"You hate it. Then change it, purify yourself; and as you are purified, you will gain wisdom. Look at your life, my dear sir. How have you spent it? In wild debauchery, receiving everything from society and giving nothing in return. You became the owner of a great fortune. How have you used it? What have you done for your neighbor? Have you ever thought about your tens of thousands of slaves? Have you helped them physically or morally? No! You have profited by their labor to lead a dissolute life. That is what you have done. Have you chosen a role in which you could serve your neighbor? No! You have spent your life in idleness. Then you married, my dear sir — took on responsibility for guiding a young woman — and what have you done? You didn't help her find the path of truth, my dear sir. You pushed her into an abyss of deceit and misery. A man insulted you and you shot him, and you say you don't know God and hate your life. That's not surprising, my dear sir!"

After these words, the Mason, as if tired from his long speech, again leaned back on the sofa and closed his eyes. Pierre stared at that aged, stern, almost lifeless face and moved his lips without making a sound. He wanted to say, "Yes, a vile, idle, sinful life!" — but didn't dare break the silence.
The Mason cleared his throat hoarsely, the way old men do, and called his servant.
"How about the horses?" he asked, without looking at Pierre.
"The fresh horses have just arrived," the servant answered. "Will you rest here?"
"No, tell them to harness up."

"Can he really be leaving — leaving me alone without telling me everything, without promising to help me?" thought Pierre, rising with bowed head. He began pacing the room, glancing occasionally at the Mason. "Yes, I never thought about it, but I have led a contemptible, dissolute life, even though I didn't want to and didn't enjoy it," thought Pierre. "But this man knows the truth, and if he wanted to, he could reveal it to me."

Pierre wanted to say this to the Mason but didn't dare. The traveler, having packed his things with practiced hands, began buttoning his coat. When he was ready, he turned to Bezukhov and said with indifferent politeness:
"Where are you headed now, my dear sir?"

"I? I'm going to Petersburg," answered Pierre in a childlike, hesitant voice. "I thank you. I agree with everything you've said. But don't think I'm as bad as all that. With all my heart I want to be what you would have me be, but I've never had help from anyone. And it's I, more than anyone, who am to blame for everything. Help me, teach me, and perhaps I might..."
Pierre couldn't go on. He choked up and turned away.
The Mason was silent for a long time, evidently thinking.

"Help comes from God alone," he said, "but whatever measure of help our Order can give, it will offer you, my dear sir. You are going to Petersburg. Give this to Count Willarski." He took out his notebook and wrote a few words on a large sheet of paper folded in four. "Allow me to offer you a piece of advice. When you reach the capital, devote some time first to solitude and self-examination, and do not return to your old way of life. And now, I wish you a good journey, my dear sir," he added, seeing that his servant had come in, "and success."

The traveler was Joseph Alexeevich Bazdeev, as Pierre saw from the postmaster's register. Bazdeev had been one of the most famous Freemasons and Martinists, even in Novikov's time. For a long while after he had gone, Pierre did not go to bed or order horses, but paced up and down the room, pondering his corrupt past and — with a joyful sense of beginning anew — picturing to himself the blissful, blameless, virtuous future that seemed so easy to achieve. It seemed to him that he had been wicked only because he had somehow forgotten how good it is to be virtuous. Not a trace of his former doubts remained in his soul. He firmly believed in the possibility of a brotherhood of men united in the pursuit of virtue, and that is how Freemasonry appeared to him.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: On arriving in Petersburg, Pierre told no one of his return. He went nowhere and spent entire days reading Thomas a Kempis, whose book had been sent to him by an unknown person. One thing he continually grasped as he read: the joy, previously unknown to him, of believing in the possibility of attaining perfection and in the possibility of active brotherly love among men, which Joseph Alexeevich had revealed to him. A week after his arrival, the young Polish count Willarski — whom Pierre had known slightly in Petersburg society — came to his room one evening with an official, ceremonious manner, much like the way Dolokhov's second had called on him. Closing the door behind him and making sure they were alone, he addressed Pierre.

"I have come to you with a message and an offer, Count," he said without sitting down. "A person of very high standing in our Brotherhood has applied for you to be received into our Order ahead of the usual schedule, and has asked me to be your sponsor. I consider it a sacred duty to fulfill that person's wishes. Do you wish to join the Brotherhood of Freemasons under my sponsorship?"
The cold, austere tone of this man — whom Pierre had almost always seen at balls, smiling pleasantly among the most brilliant women — surprised him.
"Yes, I do wish it," said he.
Willarski bowed his head.
"One more question, Count," he said, "which I beg you to answer with complete sincerity — not as a future Mason but as an honest man. Have you renounced your former beliefs? Do you believe in God?"
Pierre paused to think.
"Yes... yes, I believe in God," he said.
"In that case..." Willarski began, but Pierre interrupted him.
"Yes, I do believe in God," he repeated.
"In that case, we can go," said Willarski. "My carriage is at your service."

Willarski was silent throughout the drive. When Pierre asked what he must do and how he should answer, Willarski only replied that brothers worthier than himself would test him, and that Pierre need only tell the truth.

Having entered the courtyard of a large house where the Lodge had its headquarters, and having climbed a dark staircase, they entered a small well-lit anteroom where they removed their cloaks without a servant's help. From there they passed into another room. A man in strange attire appeared at the door. Willarski stepped toward him, said something in French in an undertone, then went to a small wardrobe in which Pierre noticed garments he had never seen before. Taking a kerchief from the cupboard, Willarski blindfolded Pierre and tied it in a knot behind his head, catching some hairs painfully in the knot. Then he pulled Pierre's face down, kissed him, and taking him by the hand, led him forward. The hair caught in the knot hurt Pierre, and there were lines of pain on his face along with an embarrassed smile. His huge figure, arms hanging at his sides, with a puckered yet smiling face, moved after Willarski with uncertain, timid steps.
Having led him about ten paces, Willarski stopped.

"Whatever happens to you," he said, "you must bear it all bravely if you have firmly resolved to join our Brotherhood." Pierre nodded. "When you hear a knock at the door, you will uncover your eyes," Willarski added. "I wish you courage and success." And pressing Pierre's hand, he went out.

Left alone, Pierre continued smiling in the same way. Once or twice he shrugged and raised his hand to the blindfold as if to take it off, but let it drop again. The five minutes he spent blindfolded seemed like an hour. His arms went numb, his legs nearly gave way — he felt utterly exhausted. He experienced a whole range of complex sensations. He was afraid of what would happen to him, and even more afraid of showing his fear. He was curious to know what was coming and what would be revealed; but most of all, he felt joyful that the moment had arrived when he would finally set out on that path of regeneration and the actively virtuous life he had been dreaming of since meeting Joseph Alexeevich. Loud knocks sounded at the door. Pierre removed the blindfold and looked around. The room was in complete darkness; only a small lamp burned inside something white. Pierre went closer and saw that the lamp stood on a black table on which lay an open book. The book was the Gospel, and the white thing with the lamp inside was a human skull with its cavities and teeth. After reading the first words of the Gospel — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" — Pierre went around the table and saw a large open box filled with something. It was a coffin containing bones. He was not at all surprised by what he saw. Hoping to begin an entirely new life, completely unlike the old, he expected everything to be unusual — even more unusual than what he was seeing. A skull, a coffin, the Gospel — he felt he had expected all this, and even more. Trying to stir his emotions, he looked around. "God, death, love, the brotherhood of man," he kept telling himself, linking these words with vague yet joyful ideas. The door opened and someone came in.

By the dim light, to which Pierre's eyes had already adjusted, he saw a rather short man. Having obviously come from a bright room into the darkness, the man paused, then moved with cautious steps toward the table and placed his small leather-gloved hands on it.

This short man wore a white leather apron covering his chest and part of his legs; around his neck was a kind of necklace above which rose a high white ruffle, framing his rather long face that was lit from below.

"Why have you come here?" asked the newcomer, turning toward Pierre at a slight rustle. "Why have you, who do not believe in the truth of the light and who have not seen the light, come here? What do you seek from us? Wisdom, virtue, enlightenment?"

The moment the door opened and the stranger entered, Pierre felt a sense of awe and reverence such as he had experienced as a boy at confession. He felt himself in the presence of someone completely unknown socially, yet closer to him through the brotherhood of man. With bated breath and pounding heart, he moved toward the Rhetor (the name given to the brother who prepares a seeker for entrance into the Brotherhood). Drawing nearer, he recognized in the Rhetor a man he knew — Smolyaninov — and it embarrassed him to think that the newcomer was an acquaintance; he wished him to be simply a brother and a virtuous teacher. For a long time he could not utter a word, so that the Rhetor had to repeat his question.
"Yes... I... I... desire regeneration," Pierre managed with difficulty.
"Very well," said Smolyaninov, and went on at once: "Have you any idea of the means by which our holy Order will help you reach your aim?" he asked quietly and quickly.
"I... hope... for guidance... help... in regeneration," said Pierre, his voice trembling with emotion and with the difficulty of speaking about abstract matters in Russian.
"What is your understanding of Freemasonry?"

"I imagine that Freemasonry is the fraternity and equality of men who share virtuous aims," said Pierre, feeling ashamed of how inadequate his words were for the solemnity of the moment. "I imagine..."
"Good!" said the Rhetor quickly, apparently satisfied with this answer. "Have you sought the means of attaining your aim in religion?"
"No, I considered it false and did not follow it," said Pierre so softly that the Rhetor didn't hear and asked him to repeat. "I have been an atheist," Pierre answered.
"You seek truth in order to follow its laws in your life, and therefore you seek wisdom and virtue. Is that not so?" said the Rhetor after a moment's pause.
"Yes, yes," Pierre agreed.
The Rhetor cleared his throat, crossed his gloved hands on his chest, and began to speak.

"Now I must reveal to you the chief aim of our Order," he said, "and if this aim matches yours, you may join our Brotherhood with profit. The first and principal object of our Order — the foundation on which it rests and which no human power can destroy — is the preservation and transmission to future generations of a certain important mystery that has come down to us from the most ancient times, from the first man himself — a mystery on which perhaps the fate of mankind depends. But since this mystery is of such a nature that no one can know or use it unless he is prepared by long and diligent self-purification, not everyone can hope to attain it quickly. So we have a secondary aim: to prepare our members as much as possible to reform their hearts, to purify and enlighten their minds, by means handed down to us by tradition from those who have striven to attain this mystery, and thereby to make them capable of receiving it.

"Through purifying and regenerating our members, we try, thirdly, to improve the whole human race, offering it in our members an example of devotion and virtue, and thereby striving with all our might to combat the evil that holds sway in the world. Think this over, and I will come to you again."

"To combat the evil that holds sway in the world..." Pierre repeated, and a mental picture of his future work in this cause rose in his mind. He imagined men like himself as he had been two weeks ago, and he pictured himself delivering an uplifting speech to them. He imagined wicked, unfortunate people whom he would help with words and actions, imagined oppressors whose victims he would rescue. Of the three aims the Rhetor had mentioned, this last — improving mankind — especially appealed to Pierre. The important mystery, though it aroused his curiosity, did not seem essential to him; and the second aim, that of purifying and regenerating himself, did not interest him much either, because at that moment he felt with delight that he was already perfectly cured of his old faults and ready for all that was good.

Half an hour later, the Rhetor returned to tell Pierre about the seven virtues, corresponding to the seven steps of Solomon's temple, which every Freemason should cultivate: 1. Discretion — the keeping of the Order's secrets. 2. Obedience to those of higher rank. 3. Morality. 4. Love of mankind. 5. Courage. 6. Generosity. 7. The love of death.

"Seventhly, try, through frequent contemplation of death," the Rhetor said, "to come to regard it not as a dreaded enemy but as a friend — one that frees the soul, weary from the labors of virtue, from this painful life and leads it to its place of reward and peace."

"Yes, that must be so," thought Pierre, after the Rhetor went away, leaving him to solitary meditation. "It must be so, but I'm still so weak that I love my life, whose meaning is only now gradually revealing itself to me." But five of the other virtues — which Pierre recalled, counting them on his fingers — he felt already in his soul: courage, generosity, morality, love of mankind, and especially obedience — which didn't even seem like a virtue to him, but a joy. He was so glad to be free from his own lawlessness and to submit his will to those who knew the unquestionable truth. He forgot what the seventh virtue was and couldn't recall it.
The third time the Rhetor returned more quickly and asked Pierre whether he was still firm in his intention and willing to submit to everything required of him.
"I am ready for anything," said Pierre.

"I must also tell you," said the Rhetor, "that our Order delivers its teaching not only in words but also by other means, which may have a stronger effect on the sincere seeker after wisdom than mere words. This room and everything you see in it should already have spoken to your heart, if it is sincere, more powerfully than words could. You will perhaps encounter a similar method of instruction in your further initiation. Our Order follows the ancient societies that conveyed their teaching through hieroglyphics. A hieroglyph," said the Rhetor, "is a symbol of something that cannot be perceived by the senses but possesses qualities resembling those of the symbol."
Pierre knew perfectly well what a hieroglyph was, but didn't dare say so. He listened to the Rhetor in silence, sensing that his ordeal was about to begin.
"If you are resolved, I must begin your initiation," said the Rhetor, coming closer to Pierre. "As a token of generosity, I ask you to give me all your valuables."
"But I have nothing here," replied Pierre, thinking he was being asked to give up everything he owned.
"What you have with you: watch, money, rings..."
Pierre quickly took out his purse and watch, but struggled for some time to get the wedding ring off his fat finger. When that was done, the Rhetor said:
"As a token of obedience, I ask you to undress."

Pierre took off his coat, waistcoat, and left boot as the Rhetor directed. The Mason pulled back Pierre's shirt from his left breast and, stooping, rolled up the left leg of his trousers above the knee. Pierre hurriedly began removing his right boot too and was about to tuck up the other trouser leg, but the Mason told him that wasn't necessary and gave him a slipper for his left foot. With a childlike smile of embarrassment, doubt, and self-mockery that appeared on his face despite himself, Pierre stood with his arms hanging down and legs apart before the Rhetor, awaiting further instructions.
"And now, as a token of candor, I ask you to reveal to me your chief weakness," said the Rhetor.
"My weakness! I have had so many," replied Pierre.
"The weakness that more than any other caused you to stray from the path of virtue," said the Mason.
Pierre hesitated, searching for an answer.
"Wine? Gluttony? Idleness? Laziness? Irritability? Anger? Women?" He ran through his vices in his mind, not knowing which to single out.
"Women," he said in a low, barely audible voice.
The Mason did not move and said nothing for a long time. At last he stepped up to Pierre and, taking the kerchief that lay on the table, blindfolded him once more.

"For the last time I say to you: turn all your attention upon yourself, put a bridle on your senses, and seek happiness not in passion but in your own heart. The source of happiness is not outside us but within."
Pierre had already long been feeling within himself that refreshing source of happiness, which now flooded his heart with joyful emotion.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The day after his initiation into the Lodge, Pierre sat at home reading a book and trying to understand the significance of the Square, one side of which symbolized God, another moral things, a third physical things, and the fourth a combination of these. Now and then his attention drifted from the book and the Square, and he found himself imagining a new plan for his life. At the Lodge the previous evening, he had heard that rumors of his duel had reached the Emperor, and that it would be wise for him to leave Petersburg. Pierre planned to go to his southern estates and attend to the welfare of his serfs. He was happily envisioning this new life when Prince Vasili suddenly walked into the room.

"My dear fellow, what have you been up to in Moscow? Why have you fallen out with Helene, mon cher? You're mistaken," said Prince Vasili as he entered. "I know all about it, and I can tell you with certainty that Helene is as innocent before you as Christ was before the Jews."
Pierre was about to reply, but Prince Vasili cut him off.

"And why didn't you simply come straight to me, as a friend? I know everything and I understand it all," he said. "You acted as a man of honor should — perhaps too hastily, but let's not get into that. But think of the position in which you're placing her and me in the eyes of society, and even of the court," he added, lowering his voice. "She's living in Moscow and you're here. Remember, dear boy" — and he pulled Pierre's arm down — "it's simply a misunderstanding. I'm sure you feel that yourself. Let's write her a letter right now, and she'll come here and everything will be cleared up — otherwise, my dear boy, I must warn you that you'll likely have to pay the consequences."
Prince Vasili gave Pierre a meaningful look.
"I know from reliable sources that the Dowager Empress is taking a keen interest in the whole affair. You know how fond she is of Helene."

Pierre tried several times to speak, but on one hand Prince Vasili wouldn't let him get a word in, and on the other, Pierre himself was afraid to begin speaking in the tone of firm refusal and disagreement he had resolved to use with his father-in-law. Moreover, the words of the Masonic statutes — "be kind and courteous" — kept echoing in his mind. He blinked, went red, got up, sat down again, struggling to do the hardest thing in the world for him — to say something unpleasant to someone's face, to say what the other person didn't expect. He was so accustomed to submitting to Prince Vasili's breezy self-assurance that he felt he would be unable to resist it now; yet he also felt that everything depended on what he said at this moment — whether he would go on in the same old rut or take that new path so attractively shown him by the Masons, on which he firmly believed he would be reborn.
"Now, dear boy," said Prince Vasili playfully, "just say 'yes,' and I'll write to her myself, and we'll kill the fatted calf."
But before Prince Vasili could finish his playful speech, Pierre — without looking at him, and with a kind of fury that made him resemble his father — muttered in a whisper:
"Prince, I did not invite you here. Go. Please go!" And he jumped up and opened the door for him.
"Go!" he repeated, astonished at himself and glad to see the look of confusion and fear on Prince Vasili's face.
"What's the matter with you? Are you ill?"
"Go!" the trembling voice repeated. And Prince Vasili had to leave without any explanation.

A week later, Pierre, having said goodbye to his new friends the Masons and leaving large sums of money with them for charitable works, departed for his estates. His new brothers gave him letters of introduction to the Kiev and Odessa Masons and promised to write to him and guide him in his new endeavors.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: The duel between Pierre and Dolokhov was hushed up, and despite the Emperor's strict stance on duels at that time, neither the principals nor their seconds suffered any consequences. But the story of the duel, compounded by Pierre's split with his wife, became the talk of society. Pierre — who had been treated with patronizing condescension as an illegitimate son, and then fussed over and flattered as the best match in Russia — had sunk greatly in society's estimation after his marriage, when the eligible daughters and their mothers had nothing more to hope from him — especially as he neither knew how nor wished to court public favor. Now he alone was blamed for what had happened; he was said to be insanely jealous and subject, like his father, to fits of bloodthirsty rage. And when Helene returned to Petersburg after Pierre's departure, she was received by all her acquaintances not only warmly but even with a touch of deference befitting her misfortune. When her husband came up in conversation, Helene assumed an expression of dignified composure — which, with her characteristic tact, she had cultivated despite not understanding its full significance. This expression suggested that she had resolved to bear her trials without complaint and that her husband was a cross laid upon her by God. Prince Vasili expressed his views more openly. He shrugged whenever Pierre was mentioned and, tapping his forehead, remarked:
"A bit touched — I always said so."

"I said it from the very beginning," declared Anna Pavlovna, referring to Pierre. "I said at the time, before anyone else" — she insisted on her priority — "that this reckless young man had been spoiled by the corrupt ideas of the age. I said so even when everyone was raving about him, when he had just returned from abroad and was posing as a sort of Marat at one of my soirees. And how has it ended? I was against this marriage from the start and predicted exactly what has happened."

Anna Pavlovna continued to host on her free evenings the same kind of soirees as before — the kind only she had the gift of arranging — where one could find "the cream of truly good society, the finest intellectual essence of Petersburg," as she put it. Besides this carefully curated selection, Anna Pavlovna's gatherings were also notable for the fact that she always presented some new and interesting person to the company, and that nowhere else was the political temperature of legitimate Petersburg court society so clearly and precisely registered.

Toward the end of 1806, when all the grim details had arrived of Napoleon's destruction of the Prussian army at Jena and Auerstadt and the surrender of most of the Prussian fortresses, when Russian troops had already entered Prussia and the second war with Napoleon was beginning, Anna Pavlovna held one of her soirees. The "cream of truly good society" consisted of the fascinating Helene, abandoned by her husband; Mortemart; the delightful Prince Hippolyte, just back from Vienna; two diplomats; the old aunt; a young man referred to in that drawing room as "a man of great merit"; a newly appointed maid of honor and her mother; and several other less notable guests.

The novelty Anna Pavlovna was serving up to her guests that evening was Boris Drubetskoy, who had just arrived as a special courier from the Prussian army and was aide-de-camp to a very important personage.
The temperature shown by the political thermometer that evening was as follows:

"Whatever the European sovereigns and commanders may do to appease Bonaparte, and to cause us annoyance and humiliation, our opinion of Bonaparte cannot change. We will not stop expressing our honest views on the matter, and can only say to the King of Prussia and the rest: 'So much the worse for you. Tu l'as voulu, George Dandin' — that's all we have to say about it!"

When Boris — who was to be the evening's main attraction — entered the drawing room, almost the entire company had assembled, and the conversation, guided by Anna Pavlovna, was focused on Russia's diplomatic relations with Austria and the hope of an alliance.

Boris, looking more grown-up and appearing fresh, rosy, and self-assured, entered the drawing room elegantly dressed in his aide-de-camp uniform. He was duly led over to pay his respects to the aunt and then brought back to the general circle.
Anna Pavlovna offered him her thin, shriveled hand to kiss and introduced him to several people he didn't know, giving him a whispered description of each.

"Prince Hippolyte Kuragin — charming young man. Monsieur Kronq — charge d'affaires from Copenhagen — a profound intellect." And simply: "Mr. Shitov — a man of great merit" — this of the man usually described that way.

Thanks to Anna Mikhailovna's efforts, his own instincts, and the peculiarities of his reserved temperament, Boris had managed during his military service to position himself very advantageously. He was aide-de-camp to a very important personage, had been sent on a very important mission to Prussia, and had just returned as a special courier. He had thoroughly mastered that unwritten code he had been so pleased to discover at Olmutz — the code by which an ensign could outrank a general, and success in the service depended not on effort or work, or courage or perseverance, but simply on knowing how to get along with those who dispense rewards. He was often surprised at how rapidly he advanced and at others' inability to grasp these principles. As a result, his entire manner of life, all his old friendships, all his plans for the future, had completely changed. He was not rich, but would spend his last ruble to be better dressed than others, and would sooner deny himself many pleasures than be seen in a shabby carriage or an old uniform. He cultivated friendships only with those above him in position who might be useful. He liked Petersburg and looked down on Moscow. His memories of the Rostov household and his boyhood love for Natasha were unpleasant to him, and he had not once visited the Rostovs since the day he left for the army. To be at Anna Pavlovna's drawing room he considered an important career advance, and he immediately understood his role, letting his hostess make use of whatever interest he could offer. He himself carefully assessed each face, evaluating the potential for forming connections with each person present and the advantages that might result. He took the seat indicated beside the beautiful Helene and listened to the general conversation.

"Vienna considers the terms of the proposed treaty so unattainable that not even a series of the most brilliant successes would secure them, and she doubts we have the means to achieve them. That is the exact phrase used by the Vienna cabinet," said the Danish charge d'affaires.
"The doubt is flattering," said "the man of profound intellect," with a subtle smile.
"We must distinguish between the Vienna cabinet and the Emperor of Austria," said Mortemart. "The Emperor of Austria could never have thought of such a thing; it's only the cabinet that says it."

"Ah, my dear vicomte," Anna Pavlovna chimed in, "L'Urope" — for some reason she pronounced it Urope, as if this were a specially refined French pronunciation she could permit herself when speaking with a Frenchman — "L'Urope ne sera jamais notre alliee sincere."
"Europe will never be our sincere ally."
After that, Anna Pavlovna steered the conversation to the courage and steadfastness of the King of Prussia, in order to draw Boris in.

Boris listened attentively to each speaker, waiting for his turn, but managed meanwhile to glance repeatedly at his neighbor, the beautiful Helene, whose eyes several times met the handsome young aide-de-camp's with a smile.

Speaking of Prussia's situation, Anna Pavlovna very naturally asked Boris to tell them about his trip to Glogau and the condition of the Prussian army. Boris spoke with deliberation in pure, correct French, sharing many interesting details about the armies and the court, carefully avoiding any expression of personal opinion about the facts he recounted. For some time he held everyone's attention, and Anna Pavlovna felt that the novelty she had served up was being enjoyed by all her guests. The person who paid the greatest attention to Boris's account was Helene. She asked him several questions about his travels and seemed deeply interested in the state of the Prussian army. As soon as he finished, she turned to him with her usual smile.
"You absolutely must come see me," she said in a tone implying that, for reasons he could not yet know, this was absolutely necessary.
"On Tuesday between eight and nine. It will give me great pleasure."
Boris promised to comply and was about to start a conversation with her when Anna Pavlovna called him away on the pretext that her aunt wished to hear him.

"You know her husband, of course?" said Anna Pavlovna, closing her eyes and gesturing sadly toward Helene. "Oh, she is such an unfortunate and charming woman! Don't mention him in front of her — please don't! It's too painful for her!"

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: When Boris and Anna Pavlovna returned to the others, Prince Hippolyte had captured the group's attention.
Leaning forward in his armchair, he said: "Le Roi de Prusse!" — and having said this, he laughed. Everyone turned toward him.

"Le Roi de Prusse?" Hippolyte repeated questioningly, laughing again, and then calmly and seriously sat back in his chair. Anna Pavlovna waited for him to continue, but as he seemed quite determined to say nothing more, she began telling how at Potsdam the godless Bonaparte had stolen the sword of Frederick the Great.

"It is the sword of Frederick the Great which I..." she began, but Hippolyte interrupted her with the words: "Le Roi de Prusse..." and again, as soon as everyone turned to look at him, excused himself and said nothing more.
Anna Pavlovna frowned. Mortemart, Hippolyte's friend, addressed him firmly.
"Come now, what about your Roi de Prusse?"
Hippolyte laughed, as if embarrassed by his own laughter.
"Oh, it's nothing. I only wanted to say..." — he had been trying all evening to work in a joke he'd heard in Vienna — "I only wanted to say that we are wrong to fight pour le Roi de Prusse!"
Boris smiled cautiously, in a way that could be taken as either ironic or appreciative, depending on how the joke landed. Everyone laughed.
"Your joke is dreadful — it's witty but unfair," said Anna Pavlovna, shaking her little shriveled finger at him.
"We are not fighting pour le Roi de Prusse, but for just principles. Oh, that wicked Prince Hippolyte!" she said.
The conversation flowed all evening, turning mainly on political news. It became particularly lively toward the end when the subject of imperial honors and awards came up.
"You know that N— N— received a snuffbox with the portrait last year?" said "the man of profound intellect." "Why shouldn't S— S— receive the same distinction?"
"I beg your pardon! A snuffbox with the Emperor's portrait is a reward, not a distinction," said the diplomat. "It's a gift, rather."
"There are precedents. I could mention Schwarzenberg."
"It's impossible," replied another.
"Will you bet? The ribbon of the order is a different matter..."
When everyone rose to leave, Helene — who had said very little all evening — turned to Boris again, asking him in a tone of caressing yet commanding significance to come to her on Tuesday.
"It's very important to me," she said, turning with a smile to Anna Pavlovna, who, with the same sad smile she wore when speaking of her exalted patroness, seconded Helene's wish.

It seemed as though something Boris had said that evening about the Prussian army had suddenly made Helene feel it was essential to see him. She seemed to promise she would explain this necessity when he came on Tuesday.

But on Tuesday evening, when Boris arrived at Helene's splendid salon, he received no clear explanation of why it had been so necessary for him to come. Other guests were there, and the countess spoke little to him. Only as he kissed her hand on leaving did she say unexpectedly, in a whisper, her face suddenly serious and unsmiling: "Come to dinner tomorrow... in the evening. You must come. Come!"
During that stay in Petersburg, Boris became a regular in the countess's household.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: The war was blazing and drawing nearer to the Russian frontier. Everywhere one heard curses against Bonaparte, "the enemy of mankind." Militia members and recruits were being enrolled in the villages, and from the front came contradictory news — false as usual, and therefore interpreted in every possible way. The life of old Prince Bolkonski, Prince Andrew, and Princess Mary had changed greatly since 1805.

In 1806 the old prince was made one of eight commanders in chief appointed to oversee the recruitment decreed throughout Russia. Despite the weakness of age — which had become especially noticeable since the time he thought his son had been killed — he did not feel right about refusing a duty the Emperor himself had assigned him, and this fresh opportunity for action gave him new energy and strength. He was constantly traveling through the three provinces entrusted to him, was meticulous to the point of tyranny with his subordinates, and personally looked into every detail. Princess Mary had stopped taking mathematics lessons from her father, and when the old prince was home she would go to his study with the wet nurse and little Prince Nicholas (as his grandfather called him). Baby Nicholas lived with his wet nurse and nanny Savishna in the late princess's rooms, and Princess Mary spent most of the day in the nursery, doing her best to take a mother's place with her little nephew. Mademoiselle Bourienne, too, seemed passionately fond of the boy, and Princess Mary often gave up her own time so her friend could have the pleasure of cuddling the little angel — as she called her nephew — and playing with him.

Near the altar of the church at Bald Hills there was a chapel over the tomb of the little princess, with a marble monument brought from Italy representing an angel with outspread wings ready to fly upward. The angel's upper lip was slightly raised as though about to smile, and once, on coming out of the chapel, Prince Andrew and Princess Mary admitted to each other that the angel's face reminded them uncannily of the little princess. But what was stranger still — though Prince Andrew said nothing about it to his sister — was that in the expression the sculptor had happened to give the angel's face, he read the same gentle reproach he had seen on the face of his dead wife: "Oh, why have you done this to me?"

Soon after Prince Andrew's return, the old prince gave him a large estate, Bogucharovo, about twenty-five miles from Bald Hills. Partly because of the painful memories associated with Bald Hills, partly because Prince Andrew didn't always feel up to bearing his father's eccentricities, and partly because he needed solitude, he began building at Bogucharovo and spent most of his time there.

After the Austerlitz campaign, Prince Andrew had firmly resolved not to continue his military service, and when the war resumed and everyone had to serve, he took a position under his father in the recruitment office so as to avoid active duty. The old man and his son seemed to have swapped roles since the 1805 campaign. The old prince, energized by activity, expected the best from the new campaign, while Prince Andrew, taking no part in the war and secretly regretting it, saw only the dark side.

On February 26, 1807, the old prince set off on one of his tours of inspection. Prince Andrew remained at Bald Hills as usual during his father's absence. Little Nicholas had been unwell for four days. The coachman who had driven the old prince to town returned with papers and letters for Prince Andrew.
Not finding the young prince in his study, the valet took the letters to Princess Mary's rooms, but didn't find him there either. He was told that the prince had gone to the nursery.
