"If you please, your excellency, Petrusha has brought some papers," said one of the nursemaids to Prince Andrew, who was sitting on a child's little chair, frowning and with trembling hands, pouring drops from a medicine bottle into a glass half full of water.
"What is it?" he said irritably, and his hand shaking involuntarily, he poured too many drops into the glass. He threw the mixture on the floor and asked for more water. The maid brought it.

In the room were a child's crib, two trunks, two armchairs, a table, a child's table, and the little chair on which Prince Andrew sat. The curtains were drawn, and a single candle burned on the table, shielded by a bound music book so the light wouldn't fall on the crib.
"My dear," said Princess Mary, addressing her brother from beside the crib where she was standing, "better wait a bit... later..."
"Oh, stop it — you always talk nonsense and put things off — and this is what comes of it!" said Prince Andrew in an exasperated whisper, clearly intending to wound his sister.
"My dear, really... it's better not to wake him... he's asleep," the princess said pleadingly.
Prince Andrew got up and went on tiptoe to the little bed, glass in hand.
"Maybe we really shouldn't wake him," he said, hesitating.

"As you wish... really... I think so... but as you wish," said Princess Mary, clearly intimidated and flustered that her opinion had prevailed. She drew her brother's attention to the maid who was calling him in a whisper.

It was the second night that neither of them had slept, watching over the boy who was running a high fever. For days now, distrusting their household doctor and waiting for another they had sent for from town, they had been trying one remedy after another. Worn out by sleeplessness and anxiety, they took out their distress on each other, bickering and blaming.
"Petrusha has come with papers from your father," the maid whispered.
Prince Andrew went out.
"Damn it all!" he muttered, and after listening to the verbal instructions his father had sent and collecting the correspondence and his father's letter, he returned to the nursery.
"Well?" he asked.
"Still the same. Wait, for heaven's sake. Karl Ivanich always says sleep is more important than anything," whispered Princess Mary with a sigh.
Prince Andrew went up to the child and felt him. He was burning hot.
"To hell with you and your Karl Ivanich!" He picked up the glass with the drops and went back to the crib.
"Andrew, don't!" said Princess Mary.
But he scowled at her — angrily, though with suffering in his eyes — and leaned over the infant with the glass in his hand.
"I want to," he said. "I'm asking you — give it to him!"

Princess Mary shrugged but obediently took the glass and, calling the nurse, began giving the medicine. The child screamed hoarsely. Prince Andrew winced, clutched his head, and went out to sit on a sofa in the next room.
He still had all the letters in his hand. Opening them mechanically, he began to read. The old prince, using occasional abbreviations, wrote in his large, elongated hand on blue paper:

Have just this moment received by special messenger very joyful news — if it's not false. Bennigsen seems to have won a complete victory over Buonaparte at Eylau. In Petersburg everyone is rejoicing, and the rewards sent to the army are countless. Though he is a German — I congratulate him! I can't figure out what the commander at Korchevo — a certain Khandrikov — is up to; the additional men and provisions still haven't arrived. Gallop over to him at once and tell him I'll have his head if everything isn't there within a week. Also received another letter about the Preussisch-Eylau battle from Petenka — he took part in it — and it's all true. When mischief-makers don't meddle, even a German can beat Buonaparte. He is said to be fleeing in great disorder. Mind you gallop off to Korchevo without delay and carry out instructions!

Prince Andrew sighed and broke the seal of another envelope. It was a closely written two-page letter from Bilibin. He folded it up without reading it and reread his father's letter, which ended with: "Gallop off to Korchevo and carry out instructions!"
"No, excuse me, I'm not going anywhere until the child is better," he thought, going to the door and looking into the nursery.
Princess Mary was still standing by the crib, gently rocking the baby.

"Ah yes, and what other unpleasant thing did he write?" thought Prince Andrew, recalling his father's letter. "Yes — we've won a victory over Bonaparte, just when I'm not serving. Yes, yes, he's always mocking me. Ah, well! Let him!" And he began reading Bilibin's letter, which was written in French. He read without understanding half of it — reading only to forget, if just for a moment, what he had been thinking about so painfully, to the exclusion of everything else.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Bilibin was now at army headquarters in a diplomatic capacity, and though he wrote in French with French wit and French turns of phrase, he described the whole campaign with a fearlessly self-critical and self-mocking honesty that was genuinely Russian. Bilibin wrote that the obligation of diplomatic discretion was tormenting him, and he was grateful to have in Prince Andrew a trustworthy correspondent to whom he could vent the frustration he had accumulated watching everything that was going on in the army. The letter was old, having been written before the battle of Preussisch-Eylau.

"Since the day of our brilliant success at Austerlitz," wrote Bilibin, "as you know, my dear prince, I never leave headquarters. I have certainly developed a taste for war, which is just as well for me; what I've seen during these last three months is unbelievable.

"I'll begin at the beginning. 'The enemy of the human race,' as you know, attacks the Prussians. The Prussians are our faithful allies who have only betrayed us three times in three years. We take up their cause, but it turns out that 'the enemy of the human race' pays no attention to our fine speeches and in his rude, savage way flings himself on the Prussians without giving them time to finish their parade. In two quick moves he smashes them to bits and settles into the palace at Potsdam.

"'I most ardently desire,' writes the King of Prussia to Bonaparte, 'that Your Majesty should be received and treated in my palace in a manner agreeable to yourself, and insofar as circumstances allowed, I have hastened to take all steps to that end. May I have succeeded!' The Prussian generals pride themselves on being polite to the French and lay down their arms at the first demand.
"The head of the garrison at Glogau, with ten thousand men, asks the King of Prussia what to do if he is ordered to surrender. All of this is absolutely true.

"In short, having hoped to settle things by looking warlike, we find we've stumbled into an actual war — and what's more, a war on our own borders, with and for the King of Prussia. We have everything in perfect order; there's just one small thing missing — namely, a commander in chief. Since it was felt that the Austerlitz success might have been more decisive if the commander in chief hadn't been so young, all our octogenarians were reviewed, and of Prozorovski and Kamenski, the latter was chosen. The general arrives, Suvorov-style, in a peasant cart, and is greeted with cheers of joy and triumph.

"On the fourth, the first courier arrives from Petersburg. The mail is brought to the field marshal's room — he insists on doing everything himself. I'm called in to help sort the letters and take those meant for us. The field marshal watches and waits for letters addressed to him. We search — there are none. He grows impatient, takes over himself, and finds letters from the Emperor to Count T., Prince V., and others. Then he explodes in one of his wild rages at everyone and everything, seizes the letters, tears them open, and reads the Emperor's correspondence with other people. 'Ah! So that's how they treat me! No confidence in me! Ah, ordered to keep an eye on me! Very well! Get out, the lot of you!' So he writes the famous order of the day to General Bennigsen:

"'I am wounded and cannot ride, and therefore cannot command the army. You have brought your army corps to Pultusk, routed: here it is exposed, without fuel or forage, so something must be done. And since, as you yourself reported to Count Buxhowden yesterday, you must think of retreating to our frontier — do so today.'

"'From all my riding,' he writes to the Emperor, 'I have developed a saddle sore which, on top of all my previous travels, completely prevents my riding and commanding so vast an army. I have therefore transferred command to the general next in seniority, Count Buxhowden, having sent him my entire staff and all that goes with it, advising him that if bread is short, he should move further into the interior of Prussia, since only one day's ration remains, and in some regiments none at all, as the division commanders Ostermann and Sedmoretski have reported, and everything the peasants had has been consumed. I myself will remain in hospital at Ostrolenka until I recover. In regard to which I humbly submit my report, with the information that if the army remains in its present camp another two weeks, there won't be a single healthy man left by spring.

"'Grant an old man, who is already disgraced by his inability to carry out the great and glorious task for which he was chosen, permission to retire to his country estate. I shall await your most gracious leave here in hospital, so that I need not play the role of secretary rather than commander in the army. My departure from the army doesn't cause the slightest stir — a blind man has left it. There are thousands like me in Russia.'
"The field marshal is furious with the Emperor and punishes us all — isn't that logical?

"That's the first act. The ones that follow are naturally more interesting and entertaining. After the field marshal's departure, it turns out we are within sight of the enemy and must give battle. Buxhowden is commander in chief by seniority, but General Bennigsen doesn't quite see it that way — especially since it's his corps that faces the enemy, and he wants to seize the chance to fight a battle 'on his own hand,' as the Germans say. He does so. This is the Battle of Pultusk, which is considered a great victory but in my opinion was nothing of the sort. We civilians, as you know, have a terrible habit of judging whether a battle was won or lost based on who retreats afterward. By that measure, we lost Pultusk. In short, we retreat after the battle but send a courier to Petersburg with news of a victory, and General Bennigsen, hoping to receive the post of commander in chief as a reward, declines to hand over command to General Buxhowden. During this interregnum we embark on a very original series of maneuvers. Our aim is no longer, as it should be, to avoid or attack the enemy, but solely to avoid General Buxhowden, who by seniority ought to be our commander. We pursue this aim so energetically that after crossing an unfordable river we burn the bridges — not to escape the enemy, but Buxhowden. General Buxhowden is very nearly attacked and captured by a superior enemy force as a result of one of these maneuvers designed to avoid him. Buxhowden chases us — we run. As soon as he crosses to our side of the river, we cross back to the other. Finally our enemy Buxhowden catches us and attacks. Both generals are furious — Buxhowden challenges Bennigsen; Bennigsen has an epileptic fit. But at the critical moment, the courier who carried news of our Pultusk 'victory' to Petersburg returns bearing our appointment as commander in chief. Our first foe, Buxhowden, is vanquished, and we can turn our thoughts to the second — Bonaparte. But just then a third enemy rises before us — the Orthodox Russian soldiers, loudly demanding bread, meat, biscuits, fodder, and whatnot! The stores are empty, the roads impassable. The Orthodox begin looting on a scale our last campaign can't begin to suggest. Half the regiments form bands, roaming the countryside and putting everything to fire and sword. The inhabitants are completely ruined, the hospitals overflowing, and famine is everywhere. Twice the marauders even attack our headquarters, and the commander in chief has to call in a battalion to drive them off. During one of these raids they made off with my empty suitcase and my dressing gown. The Emperor proposes giving all division commanders the right to shoot marauders, but I very much fear this will oblige half the army to shoot the other half."

At first Prince Andrew read with only his eyes, but after a while — despite knowing how far Bilibin could be trusted — what he read began to grip him. When he had gotten this far, he crumpled the letter and threw it away. It wasn't what he had read that upset him, but the fact that life out there — in which he now had no part — could still affect him so. He closed his eyes, rubbed his forehead as if to rid himself of all interest in what he had read, and listened to what was happening in the nursery. Suddenly he thought he heard a strange noise through the door. A wave of alarm seized him — what if something had happened to the child while he was reading? He went on tiptoe to the nursery door and opened it.
Just as he entered, he saw the nurse hiding something from him with a frightened expression, and Princess Mary was no longer by the crib.
"My dear," he heard what sounded like her despairing whisper behind him.

As often happens after prolonged sleeplessness and anxiety, he was seized by irrational panic — the thought struck him that the child was dead. Everything he saw and heard seemed to confirm this terror.

"It's all over," he thought, and cold sweat broke out on his forehead. He went to the crib in confusion, certain he would find it empty and that the nurse had been hiding the dead baby. He pulled the curtain aside, and for a while his frightened, restless eyes could not find the child. At last he saw him: the rosy boy had tossed about until he lay sideways across the bed with his head lower than the pillow, smacking his lips in his sleep and breathing evenly.

Prince Andrew was as overjoyed to see the boy like this as if he had already lost him. He bent over and, as his sister had taught him, tried with his lips to check whether the child was still feverish. The soft forehead was damp. Prince Andrew touched the head with his hand — even the hair was wet, so profusely had the child perspired. He was not dead; clearly the crisis had passed and he was getting better. Prince Andrew longed to snatch up this helpless little creature, to squeeze him, to hold him against his heart — but he didn't dare. He stood over him, gazing at the small head and the little arms and legs poking out from under the blanket. He heard a movement behind him and a shadow fell across the curtain of the crib. He didn't look around but kept watching the infant's face and listening to his steady breathing. The dark shadow was Princess Mary, who had come up with noiseless steps, lifted the curtain, and let it fall behind her. Prince Andrew recognized her without looking and reached out his hand. She pressed it.
"He's perspired," said Prince Andrew.
"I was coming to tell you."
The child stirred slightly in his sleep, smiled, and rubbed his forehead against the pillow.

Prince Andrew looked at his sister. In the dim shadow of the curtain, her luminous eyes shone more brightly than usual from the tears of joy in them. She leaned over and kissed her brother, slightly brushing the curtain of the crib. Each made a warning gesture to the other, and they stood still in the faint light beneath the curtain, as if not wanting to leave this cocoon where the three of them were sealed off from all the world. Prince Andrew was the first to move away, ruffling his hair against the muslin.
"Yes, this is the one thing left to me now," he said with a sigh.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Returning from his tour of southern Russia in the happiest frame of mind, Pierre carried out an intention he had long had — visiting his friend Bolkonski, whom he hadn't seen in two years.

Bogucharovo lay in a flat, uninteresting stretch of country among fields and forests of fir and birch, partly cut down. The house stood behind a newly dug pond, filled to the brim, its banks still bare. It was at the end of a village that stretched along the highway, in the middle of a young copse dotted with a few fir trees.

The homestead consisted of a threshing floor, outbuildings, stables, a bathhouse, a lodge, and a large brick house with a semicircular facade, still under construction. Around it was a newly laid-out garden. The fences and gates were new and solid; two fire pumps and a water cart, painted green, stood in a shed; the paths were straight, the bridges strong and had handrails. Everything bore the stamp of tidiness and good management. Some household serfs Pierre met, in reply to his question about where the prince lived, pointed to a small, recently built lodge near the pond. Anton, the man who had looked after Prince Andrew since childhood, helped Pierre out of his carriage, said the prince was home, and showed him into a clean little anteroom.
Pierre was struck by the modesty of the small but clean house after the grand surroundings in which he had last seen his friend in Petersburg.
He quickly entered the little reception room with its still-unplastered wooden walls, fragrant with pine, and would have gone farther, but Anton ran ahead on tiptoe and knocked at a door.
"Well, what is it?" came a sharp, unpleasant voice.
"A visitor," Anton answered.
"Ask him to wait," and the sound of a chair being pushed back was heard.

Pierre walked quickly to the door and came face to face with Prince Andrew, who emerged frowning and looking older. Pierre embraced him and, lifting his spectacles, kissed his friend on the cheek and studied him closely.
"Well, I didn't expect you — but I'm very glad," said Prince Andrew.

Pierre said nothing; he stared at his friend in surprise. He was struck by the change in him. His words were kind and there was a smile on his lips, but his eyes were dull and lifeless, and despite an obvious wish to appear otherwise, he couldn't give them a joyful, glad sparkle. Prince Andrew had grown thinner, paler, and more manly, but what startled and estranged Pierre — until he got used to it — were his apathy and a deep crease on his brow, the mark of prolonged concentration on a single thought.

As usually happens when people meet after a long separation, their conversation was slow to settle on anything. They asked questions and gave brief answers about topics they knew should be discussed at length. Eventually the talk gradually found its footing, touching on their past, their plans, Pierre's travels and activities, the war, and so on. The preoccupation and gloom Pierre had noticed in his friend's expression were now even more evident in the smile with which he listened — especially when Pierre spoke with happy excitement about the past or the future. It was as if Prince Andrew wanted to sympathize with what Pierre was saying but couldn't. Pierre began to feel it was in poor taste to talk about his enthusiasms, dreams, and hopes for happiness in Prince Andrew's presence. He was embarrassed to share his new Masonic views, which his recent travels had especially strengthened. He held himself back, afraid of seeming naive; and yet he felt an irresistible desire to show his friend as soon as possible that he was now a completely different and better Pierre than the one Prince Andrew had known in Petersburg.
"I can't tell you how much I've lived through since then. I hardly recognize myself."
"Yes, we've changed a great deal — very much — since then," said Prince Andrew.
"Well, and you? What are your plans?"
"Plans!" Prince Andrew repeated ironically. "My plans?" he said, as though astonished by the word. "Well, you see, I'm building. I plan to settle here for good next year..."
Pierre looked silently and searchingly into Prince Andrew's face, which had aged considerably.
"No, I meant to ask..." Pierre began, but Prince Andrew interrupted.
"But why talk about me? Tell me about yourself — about your travels and everything you've been doing on your estates."

Pierre began describing what he had done on his estates, trying as much as possible to downplay his own role in the improvements. Prince Andrew several times prompted Pierre's account, as though it were all an old, familiar story, and he listened not only without interest but as if embarrassed by what Pierre was telling him.
Pierre began to feel uncomfortable and even depressed in his friend's company, and at last fell silent.

"I'll tell you what, my dear fellow," said Prince Andrew — who also clearly felt awkward and constrained with his visitor — "I'm only camping out here and just came to look things over. I'm going back to my sister today. I'll introduce you to her. Though of course you know her already," he added, obviously trying to entertain a guest with whom he now had nothing in common. "We'll go after dinner. And would you like to look around the place now?"

They went out and walked about until dinnertime, talking about political news and mutual acquaintances like people who aren't close. Prince Andrew spoke with some energy and interest only about the new house and its construction; but even then, while standing on the scaffolding in the middle of explaining the future layout, he suddenly broke off:
"Anyway, this isn't interesting at all. Let's have dinner, and then we'll set off."
At dinner the conversation turned to Pierre's marriage.
"I was very surprised when I heard about it," said Prince Andrew.
Pierre blushed, as he always did when the subject came up, and said hurriedly: "I'll tell you someday how it all happened. But you know it's over — and forever."
"Forever?" said Prince Andrew. "Nothing is forever."
"But you know how it ended, don't you? You heard about the duel?"
"Yes, so you had to go through that too!"
"One thing I thank God for is that I didn't kill that man," said Pierre.
"Why?" asked Prince Andrew. "Killing a vicious dog is actually a good thing."
"No, killing a man is wrong — it's bad."

"Why is it wrong?" pressed Prince Andrew. "It's not given to us to know what is right and what is wrong. People always have erred and always will — and in nothing more than in what they consider right and wrong."

"What harms another person is wrong," said Pierre, pleased that for the first time since his arrival Prince Andrew was engaged, had started talking, and wanted to express what had brought him to his present state.
"And who told you what is harmful to another person?" Andrew asked.
"Bad! Bad!" exclaimed Pierre. "We all know what is bad for ourselves."

"Yes, we know that — but the harm I'm aware of in myself is something I can't inflict on others," said Prince Andrew, becoming more and more animated, clearly wanting to express his new outlook to Pierre. He switched to French. "I know only two very real evils in life: remorse and illness. The only good is the absence of those evils. To live for myself, avoiding those two evils — that's my whole philosophy now."

"And love of one's neighbor? And self-sacrifice?" Pierre began. "No, I can't agree with you! To live only so as not to do evil and not to feel regret — that's not enough. I lived like that once, I lived for myself and ruined my life. Only now, when I'm living — or at least trying" — Pierre's modesty made him correct himself — "to live for others, only now have I understood true happiness. No, I can't agree, and you don't really believe what you're saying." Prince Andrew looked at Pierre silently with an ironic smile.

"When you meet my sister — Princess Mary — you'll get along with her," he said. "Perhaps you're right, for yourself," he added after a short pause, "but everyone lives in his own way. You lived for yourself and say you nearly ruined your life and only found happiness when you started living for others. I had just the opposite experience. I lived for glory — and after all, what is glory? The same love of others, a desire to do something for them, a desire for their approval. So I lived for others, and not almost but completely ruined my life. And I've only found some peace since I began living for myself alone."
"But what do you mean by living for yourself alone?" asked Pierre, growing excited. "What about your son, your sister, your father?"

"But that's just the same as myself — they're not others," Prince Andrew explained. "Other people, one's neighbors — le prochain, as you and Princess Mary call it — are the main source of all error and evil. Le prochain — your Kiev peasants you want to do good for."
And he looked at Pierre with a mocking, challenging expression, clearly wanting to draw him out.

"You're joking," replied Pierre, growing more excited. "What error or evil can there be in my wishing to do good — and even doing a little, though I did it badly? What harm is there if unfortunate people — our serfs, people like us — were growing up and dying with no idea of God or truth beyond ceremonies and meaningless prayers, and are now learning a comforting faith in a future life, in retribution, reward, and consolation? What evil is there in providing a doctor, a hospital, and an asylum for the elderly to people who were dying of disease without any help, when such assistance is so easy to give? Isn't it an obvious, undeniable good to give rest and relief to a peasant or a mother with a baby who has no peace day or night?" said Pierre, speaking quickly, with a lisp. "And I've done that — though badly and in small measure — but I have done something, and you can't persuade me it wasn't a good thing. More than that, you can't make me believe you don't think so yourself. And the main thing," he went on, "is that I know — I know for certain — that the joy of doing good is the only sure happiness in life."

"Yes, if you put it that way, it's a different matter entirely," said Prince Andrew. "I build a house and plant a garden, and you build hospitals. Either one can serve as a pastime. But what's truly right and good can only be judged by someone who knows everything — not by us. Well, you want an argument," he added. "Come on, then."
They rose from the table and sat down in the entrance porch, which served as a veranda.

"Let's argue, then," said Prince Andrew. "You talk about schools," he went on, bending a finger, "education and the like — that is, you want to raise him" — he pointed to a peasant passing by who doffed his cap — "out of his animal condition and awaken spiritual needs in him. But it seems to me that animal happiness is the only happiness possible — and that's exactly what you want to take from him. I envy him, but you want to make him into what I am without giving him my resources. Then you say 'lighten his toil.' But as I see it, physical labor is as essential to him, as much a condition of his existence, as mental activity is to you or me. You can't help thinking. I go to bed after two in the morning, thoughts come, and I can't sleep — I toss until dawn because I think and can't stop, just as he can't stop plowing and mowing. If he didn't, he'd go to the tavern or fall sick. Just as I couldn't stand his terrible physical labor and would die within a week, he couldn't stand my idleness — he'd grow fat and die. And the third thing — what else did you mention?" He bent a third finger. "Ah, yes — hospitals, medicine. He has a seizure, he's dying, and you come along and bleed him and patch him up. He'll drag on as a cripple, a burden to everyone, for another ten years. It would be far easier and simpler for him to die. Others are being born — there are plenty as it is. It would be different if you were reluctant to lose a laborer — that's how I see him — but you want to cure him out of love. And he doesn't want that. Besides, what an idea — that medicine ever cured anyone! Killed them, yes!" he said, frowning angrily and turning away from Pierre.

Prince Andrew expressed his views so clearly and precisely that it was obvious he had thought about this at length. He spoke readily and rapidly, like a man who has not talked in a long time. His eyes grew more animated as his conclusions grew more bleak.

"Oh, that's terrible, terrible!" said Pierre. "I can't understand how one can live with such ideas. I had moments like that myself not long ago — in Moscow and while traveling — but at those times I collapsed so completely that I couldn't function, everything seemed hateful to me, myself most of all. Then I couldn't eat, couldn't wash... How is it with you?"

"Why not wash? That's unhygienic," said Prince Andrew. "On the contrary, one should try to make one's life as pleasant as possible. I'm alive — that's not my fault — so I must live out my life as best I can without hurting others."
"But with such views, what motive is there to go on living? One would just sit without moving, doing nothing..."

"Life itself doesn't leave you in peace. I'd be grateful to do nothing, but here on one hand the local nobility have done me the honor of electing me their marshal — I could barely get out of it. They couldn't understand that I lack the necessary qualities — the good-natured, fussy shallowness the job requires. Then there's this house, which has to be built to have a corner of my own for some peace. And now there's the recruiting."
"Why aren't you serving in the army?"

"After Austerlitz!" said Prince Andrew darkly. "No, thank you. I've promised myself never to serve in the active Russian army again. And I won't — not even if Bonaparte were here at Smolensk threatening Bald Hills — even then I wouldn't serve in the Russian army! Well, as I was saying," he continued, regaining his composure, "now there's the recruiting. My father is chief of the Third District, and my only way of avoiding active service is to serve under him."
"So you are serving?"
"I am."
He was quiet for a moment.
"And why do you serve?"

"For this reason: my father is one of the most remarkable men of his time. But he's growing old, and though not exactly cruel, he has too forceful a temperament. He's so accustomed to unlimited power that he's terrifying, and now he has this authority as a commander in chief of recruitment, granted by the Emperor. If I had been two hours late a couple of weeks ago, he would have had a paymaster's clerk at Yukhnovo hanged," said Prince Andrew with a smile. "So I serve because I'm the only one who has any influence over my father, and now and then I can save him from actions that would torment him afterward."
"Well, there you see!"

"Yes, but it's not the way you think," Prince Andrew continued. "I didn't and don't in the least care about that scoundrel of a clerk who stole boots from the recruits — I would actually have been glad to see him hanged. But I was sorry for my father — and that again is for my own sake."
Prince Andrew grew more and more animated. His eyes glittered feverishly as he tried to prove to Pierre that his actions contained no desire to do good for his neighbor.

"So — you want to liberate your serfs," he continued. "That's a very fine thing, but not for you — I don't suppose you've ever had anyone flogged or sent to Siberia — and still less for your serfs. If they're beaten, flogged, or sent to Siberia, I doubt they're any the worse for it. In Siberia they lead the same animal life, and the welts on their bodies heal, and they're as contented as before. But it's a good thing for the proprietors — who are destroyed morally, who bring remorse upon themselves, stifle that remorse, and grow callous as a result of having the power to punish justly and unjustly. It's those people I pity, and for their sake I would like to liberate the serfs. You may not have seen it, but I have — how good men raised in those traditions of unlimited power, as they grow more irritable with age, become cruel and harsh, know it, but can't control themselves, and grow more and more wretched."
Prince Andrew spoke so passionately that Pierre couldn't help thinking these ideas had been suggested by Prince Andrew's own father's case.
He said nothing in reply.
"So that's what I'm sorry for — human dignity, peace of mind, purity — and not the serfs' backs and foreheads, which, beat and shave them as you might, always remain the same backs and foreheads."
"No, no! A thousand times no! I will never agree with you," said Pierre.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: In the evening, Andrew and Pierre got into the open carriage and drove to Bald Hills. Prince Andrew, glancing at Pierre, broke the silence now and then with remarks that showed he was in a good mood.
Pointing to the fields, he spoke of the improvements he was making to his farming.
Pierre remained gloomily silent, answering in monosyllables, apparently absorbed in his own thoughts.

He was thinking that Prince Andrew was unhappy, that he had lost his way, that he didn't see the true light, and that he, Pierre, ought to help, enlighten, and uplift him. But the moment he considered what he should say, he felt that Prince Andrew would demolish his entire philosophy with a single word, a single argument — and so he shrank from beginning, afraid of exposing what he held sacred to possible ridicule.
"No — but why do you think that?" Pierre suddenly began, lowering his head and looking like a bull about to charge. "Why do you think that? You shouldn't think that way."
"Think? About what?" asked Prince Andrew in surprise.

"About life. About man's destiny. It can't be the way you see it. I used to think the same way, and do you know what saved me? Freemasonry! No, don't smile. Freemasonry is not a religious ceremony or a sect, as I once thought. Freemasonry is the best expression of the best and most eternal aspects of humanity."

And he began to explain Freemasonry as he understood it to Prince Andrew. He said that Freemasonry is the teaching of Christianity freed from the chains of Church and State — a teaching of equality, brotherhood, and love.

"Only our holy brotherhood possesses the real meaning of life; all the rest is a dream," said Pierre. "Understand, my dear fellow, that outside this union everything is filled with deceit and falsehood, and I agree with you that an intelligent, good man has nothing left but to live out his life trying not to hurt others. But make our fundamental convictions your own — join our brotherhood, surrender yourself to us, let yourself be guided, and you will immediately feel, as I have felt, that you are part of a vast, invisible chain whose beginning is hidden in heaven," said Pierre.

Prince Andrew, looking straight ahead, listened in silence. More than once, when the noise of the wheels kept him from catching Pierre's words, he asked him to repeat — and from the particular glow that came into his eyes and his silence, Pierre could tell his words were not in vain, and that Prince Andrew would neither interrupt nor laugh at him.
They reached a river that had overflowed its banks and had to be crossed by ferry. While the carriage and horses were being loaded onto the raft, they stepped on as well.
Prince Andrew leaned on the railing and gazed silently at the floodwaters shimmering in the setting sun.
"Well, what do you think about it?" asked Pierre. "Why are you quiet?"

"What do I think? I'm listening. It's all very well. You say: join our brotherhood and we'll show you the meaning of life, the destiny of man, and the laws that govern the world. But who are we? Human beings. How is it that you know everything? Why am I the only one who can't see what you see? You see a reign of goodness and truth on earth — but I don't."
Pierre interrupted him.
"Do you believe in a future life?" he asked.
"A future life?" Prince Andrew repeated — but Pierre, giving him no time to answer, took the repetition as a denial, all the more readily since he knew of Prince Andrew's former atheism.

"You say you can't see a kingdom of goodness and truth on earth. Neither could I — and it can't be seen if you regard this life as the end of everything. On earth — here on this earth" — Pierre pointed to the fields — "there is no truth; all is false and evil. But in the universe, in the whole universe, there is a kingdom of truth, and we who are now children of the earth are — for all eternity — children of the whole universe. Don't I feel in my soul that I am part of this vast, harmonious whole? Don't I feel that in this immense multitude of beings, in which the Divine — the Supreme Power, if you prefer — is manifest, I form one link, one step, between the lower and the higher? If I see — clearly see — a ladder leading from plant to man, why should I suppose it breaks off at me and doesn't go further and further? I feel that I cannot simply vanish, since nothing in this world vanishes, but that I shall always exist and always have existed. I feel that beyond me and above me there are spirits, and that in this world there is truth."

"Yes, that's Herder's theory," said Prince Andrew, "but it's not arguments that can convince me, dear friend — it's life and death that convince. What convinces is when you see a being dear to you, bound up with your own life, someone before whom you feel guilty and hoped to make amends" — Prince Andrew's voice trembled and he turned away — "and suddenly that being is seized with pain, suffers, and ceases to exist. Why? It cannot be that there is no answer. And I believe there is. That's what convinces — that is what has convinced me," said Prince Andrew.
"Yes, yes, of course," said Pierre. "Isn't that what I'm saying?"

"No. All I say is that it's not arguments that convince me of the necessity of a future life, but this: when you walk hand in hand with someone, and suddenly that person vanishes — into nowhere — and you're left standing before that abyss, staring into it. And I have stared into it."
"Well, that's exactly it! You know that there is a there, and there is a Someone. There is the future life. The Someone is God."

Prince Andrew did not reply. The carriage and horses had long since been taken off the raft and reharnessed on the far bank. The sun had sunk halfway below the horizon and an evening frost was glazing the puddles near the ferry, but Pierre and Andrew — to the astonishment of the footmen, coachmen, and ferrymen — still stood on the raft, talking.

"If there is a God and a future life, there is truth and goodness, and man's highest happiness lies in striving to attain them. We must live, we must love, and we must believe that we live not only today on this scrap of earth, but have lived and shall live forever — there, in the Whole," said Pierre, pointing to the sky.

Prince Andrew stood leaning on the railing, gazing at the red reflection of the sun on the blue water. There was perfect stillness. Pierre fell silent. The raft had long since stopped, and only the gentle waves of the current lapped softly against it. Prince Andrew felt as if the sound of the water was a kind of refrain to Pierre's words, whispering:
"It is true, believe it."
He sighed and looked at Pierre's flushed, enraptured face with a radiant, childlike, tender gaze — one that was also a bit shy before his more assured friend.

"Yes, if only it were so!" said Prince Andrew. "But it's time to go." And stepping off the raft, he looked up at the sky to which Pierre had pointed, and for the first time since Austerlitz he saw that high, everlasting sky he had gazed at on the battlefield; and something that had long been dormant, something that was the best in him, suddenly stirred — joyful and youthful — in his soul. It vanished as soon as he returned to the normal conditions of his life, but he knew that this feeling — which he had no idea how to nurture — existed within him. His meeting with Pierre marked a turning point in Prince Andrew's life. Though outwardly he continued to live as before, inwardly he began a new life.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: It was getting dark when Prince Andrew and Pierre drove up to the front entrance of the house at Bald Hills. As they approached, Prince Andrew pointed out with a smile a commotion at the back porch. A woman bent with age, a wallet on her back, and a short, long-haired young man in a black robe had dashed back to the gate on seeing the carriage. Two women ran out after them, and all four, glancing fearfully at the carriage, hurried up the steps of the back porch.

"Those are Mary's 'God's folk,'" said Prince Andrew. "They've mistaken us for my father. This is the one matter in which she disobeys him. He orders these pilgrims driven away, but she takes them in."
"But what are 'God's folk'?" asked Pierre.
Prince Andrew had no time to answer. The servants came out to greet them, and he asked where the old prince was and whether he was expected back soon.
The old prince had gone to town and was expected any minute.
Prince Andrew led Pierre to his own rooms — which were always kept in perfect order at his father's house — and went to the nursery.

"Let's go see my sister," he said to Pierre when he returned. "I haven't found her yet — she's hiding now, sitting with her 'God's folk.' It'll serve her right; she'll be embarrassed. But you'll see her 'God's folk.' It's really quite something."
"What are 'God's folk'?" asked Pierre.
"Come, and you'll see for yourself."

Princess Mary was indeed flustered, red patches appearing on her face, when they entered. In her cozy room, with lamps burning before the icon stand, a young man with a long nose and long hair, wearing a monk's cassock, sat on the sofa beside her, behind a samovar. Nearby in an armchair sat a thin, shriveled old woman with a meek expression on her childlike face.
"Andrew, why didn't you warn me?" said the princess, with mild reproach, as she stood before her pilgrims like a hen protecting her chicks.

"Delighted to see you. I'm very glad to see you," * she said to Pierre as he kissed her hand. She had known him as a child, and now his friendship with Andrew, his marital troubles, and above all his kind, simple face inclined her warmly toward him. She looked at him with her beautiful, radiant eyes, and seemed to say: "I like you very much, but please don't make fun of my people." After the first greetings they sat down.
"Delighted to see you. I am very glad to see you."
"Ah, and Ivanushka is here too!" said Prince Andrew, glancing with a smile at the young pilgrim.
"Andrew!" said Princess Mary imploringly. "You must know that this is a woman," * Prince Andrew said to Pierre.
"Andrew, for God's sake!" Princess Mary repeated.
"You must know that this is a woman."
"For heaven's sake."
It was clear that Prince Andrew's ironic attitude toward the pilgrims and Princess Mary's helpless attempts to shield them were their usual, long-established dynamic on this subject.
"But, my dear friend," said Prince Andrew, "on the contrary, you should be grateful that I'm explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man." *
"But, my dear, you ought on the contrary to be grateful to me for explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."

"Really?" said Pierre, peering over his spectacles with curiosity and seriousness — for which Princess Mary was especially grateful — at Ivanushka's face. Ivanushka, sensing she was being discussed, looked around at them all with sly eyes.

Princess Mary's embarrassment on behalf of her guests was quite unnecessary. They were not the least bit flustered. The old woman, eyes lowered but casting sideways glances at the newcomers, had turned her cup upside down and placed a nibbled piece of sugar beside it, sitting quietly in her armchair, clearly hoping for another cup of tea. Ivanushka, sipping from her saucer, watched the young men from under her brows with sly, feminine eyes.
"Where have you been? To Kiev?" Prince Andrew asked the old woman.

"I have, dear sir," she answered readily. "At Christmastime I was found worthy to receive the holy sacrament at the shrine of the saint. And now I've come from Kolyazin, sir, where a great and wonderful blessing has been revealed."
"And was Ivanushka with you?"
"I travel alone, kind sir," said Ivanushka, trying to speak in a bass voice. "I only ran into Pelageya at Yukhnovo."
Pelageya interrupted her companion — she obviously wanted to tell what she had seen.
"In Kolyazin, sir, a wonderful blessing has been revealed."
"What is it? Some new relics?" asked Prince Andrew.
"Andrew, please stop," said Princess Mary. "Don't tell him, Pelageya."

"No, why not, my dear? Why shouldn't I? I like him. He's kind, he's one of God's chosen, a benefactor — he once gave me ten rubles, I remember. When I was in Kiev, Holy Fool Cyril says to me — he's one of God's own, walks barefoot summer and winter — he says, 'Why aren't you going to the right place? Go to Kolyazin, where a miracle-working icon of the Holy Mother of God has been revealed.' Hearing those words, I said goodbye to the holy folk and went."
Everyone was silent; only the pilgrim woman went on in measured tones, drawing in her breath.
"So I come, sir, and the people say to me: 'A great blessing has been revealed — holy oil drips from the cheeks of our Blessed Mother, the Holy Virgin...'"
"All right, all right, you can tell us later," said Princess Mary, blushing.
"Let me ask her," said Pierre. "Did you see it yourself?"
"Oh yes, sir, I was found worthy. Such a brightness on the face, like the light of heaven, and from the Blessed Mother's cheek it drops and drops..."
"But my dear woman, that must be a fraud!" said Pierre naively, having listened attentively to the pilgrim.
"Oh sir! What are you saying?" exclaimed the horrified Pelageya, turning to Princess Mary for support.
"They're imposing on the people," Pierre repeated.

"Lord Jesus Christ!" cried the pilgrim, crossing herself. "Oh, don't say that, sir! There was a general who didn't believe — he said, 'The monks are cheating' — and the moment he said it, he went blind. And he dreamed that the Holy Virgin of the Kiev catacombs came to him and said, 'Believe in me and I will make you whole.' So he begged: 'Take me to her, take me to her.' It's the honest truth — I saw it with my own eyes. They brought him, quite blind, straight to her, and he falls down and says, 'Make me whole, and I'll give you what the Tsar gave me.' I saw it myself, sir — the star is set right into the icon. Well, and then what? He got his sight back! It's a sin to talk like that. God will punish you," she said admonishingly, turning to Pierre.
"How did the star get into the icon?" Pierre asked.
"And was the Holy Mother promoted to the rank of general?" said Prince Andrew with a smile.
Pelageya suddenly went very pale and clasped her hands.

"Oh sir, sir, what a sin! And you who have a son!" she began, her pallor flushing to vivid red. "Sir, what have you said? God forgive you!" And she crossed herself. "Lord forgive him! My dear, what does it mean?" she asked, turning to Princess Mary. She stood up and, nearly in tears, began gathering her things into her wallet. She was clearly frightened and ashamed to have accepted hospitality in a house where such things could be said, and at the same time sorry to lose the charity this house provided.
"Now, why did you have to do that?" said Princess Mary. "Why did you come to me?"

"Come, Pelageya, I was joking," said Pierre. "Princess, I give you my word, I didn't mean to offend her. * I meant nothing — I was only joking," he said, smiling shyly and trying to make amends. "It was all my fault, and Andrew was only joking."
"Princess, on my word, I did not wish to offend her."
Pelageya hesitated, but Pierre's face showed such sincere penitence, and Prince Andrew looked so gently now at her and now at Pierre, that she was gradually reassured.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: The pilgrim woman, once mollified, needed little encouragement to talk at length. She told them about Father Amphilochus, who led so holy a life that his hands smelled of incense, and how on her last visit to Kiev some monks she knew had given her the keys to the catacombs, and how she had taken some dried bread and spent two days among the saints. "I'd pray awhile to one, sit and think awhile, then move on to another. I'd sleep a bit and then go kiss the relics again, and there was such peace all around, such blessedness, that you don't want to come back out — not even into the light of heaven."
Pierre listened attentively and seriously. Prince Andrew left the room, and then — leaving "God's folk" to finish their tea — Princess Mary took Pierre into the drawing room.
"You are very kind," she said to him.
"Oh, I really didn't mean to hurt her feelings. I understand them so well and have the greatest respect for them."
Princess Mary looked at him in silence and smiled affectionately.

"I've known you a long time, you see, and love you like a brother," she said. "How do you find Andrew?" she added quickly, not giving him time to respond to her warm words. "I'm very worried about him. His health was better in winter, but last spring his wound reopened and the doctor said he should go away for treatment. And I'm also very much afraid for him spiritually. He doesn't have a temperament like us women, who can cry away our sorrows. He keeps everything locked inside. Today he's cheerful and in good spirits — but that's the effect of your visit; he's not often like this. If you could persuade him to go abroad... He needs activity, and this quiet, routine life is very bad for him. Others don't notice it, but I see it."
Around ten o'clock the servants rushed to the front door, hearing the bells of the old prince's carriage approaching. Prince Andrew and Pierre also went out to the porch.
"Who's that?" asked the old prince, noticing Pierre as he climbed out of the carriage.
"Ah! Very glad! Give me a kiss," he said, having learned who the young stranger was.
The old prince was in a good mood and very gracious to Pierre.

Before supper, Prince Andrew returned to his father's study and found him hotly debating with their guest. Pierre was arguing that a time would come when there would be no more wars. The old prince challenged him playfully but without getting angry.

"Drain the blood from men's veins and fill them with water, and then there'll be no more war! Old women's nonsense — old women's nonsense!" he repeated, but still patted Pierre affectionately on the shoulder. Then he went to the table where Prince Andrew — obviously not wanting to join the conversation — was looking through the papers his father had brought from town. The old prince came up to him and began talking business.

"The marshal — a Count Rostov — hasn't sent half his quota. He came to town and wanted to invite me to dinner — I gave him a fine dinner! And then, look at this... Well, my boy," the old prince went on, turning to his son and patting Pierre on the shoulder, "a fine fellow, your friend — I like him! He gets me going. Another man says clever things and you don't care to listen, but this one talks nonsense and stirs an old man up. Well, go on! Get along! Maybe I'll come sit with you at supper. We'll have another argument. Make friends with my little fool, Princess Mary," he shouted after Pierre through the door.

Only now, on this visit to Bald Hills, did Pierre fully appreciate the strength and charm of his friendship with Prince Andrew. That charm showed itself not so much in his relationship with Andrew as in his interactions with the whole family and household. With the stern old prince and the gentle, timid Princess Mary — though he barely knew them — Pierre immediately felt like an old friend. They were all fond of him already. Not only Princess Mary, who had been won over by his kindness to the pilgrims and now gave him her most radiant looks, but even the one-year-old "Prince Nicholas" (as his grandfather called him) smiled at Pierre and let himself be held; and Michael Ivanovich and Mademoiselle Bourienne beamed with pleasant smiles when he talked to the old prince.
The old prince came to supper — clearly on Pierre's account. And during the two days of the young man's visit, he was extremely warm and told him to come again.

When Pierre had gone and the household gathered together, they began sharing their impressions of him, as people always do after a new acquaintance has left — but as rarely happens, no one said anything but good of him.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: When Rostov returned from leave to his regiment, he felt for the first time how strong the bond was that tied him to Denisov and the regiment as a whole.

As he approached, Rostov felt the same thing he'd felt when approaching his family home in Moscow. When he spotted the first hussar in the unbuttoned uniform of his regiment, when he recognized red-haired Dementyev and saw the picket ropes of the roan horses, when Lavrushka joyfully shouted to his master, "The count has come!" and Denisov, who'd been asleep, came running out of the mud hut all disheveled to embrace him, and the officers crowded around to greet the new arrival — Rostov felt the same emotion as when his mother, father, and sister had embraced him. Tears of joy choked him so that he couldn't speak. The regiment was also a home, and one as unchangeably dear and precious as his parents' house.

When he had reported to the regimental commander and been reassigned to his old squadron, when he'd been on duty and gone out foraging, when he had re-entered all the small concerns of regimental life and felt himself stripped of liberty and bound in one narrow, fixed frame — he experienced the same sense of peace, of moral grounding, of being at home in his proper place, as he had felt under his parents' roof. Gone was all the chaos of the wider world, where he didn't know where he belonged and made wrong decisions; gone was Sonya, with whom he needed to have — or not have — an explanation; gone was the possibility of going here or there; gone were those twenty-four hours a day that could be spent in so many different ways; gone was that enormous crowd of people, none of them closer or more distant than any other; gone were those uncertain, murky money matters with his father, and any thought of that terrible debt to Dolokhov. Here in the regiment everything was clear and simple. The whole world was divided into two unequal parts: one was the Pavlograd regiment; the other was everything else — and the rest was none of his concern. In the regiment, everything was defined: who was a lieutenant, who a captain, who was a good fellow and who wasn't, and above all, who was a comrade. The canteen keeper gave you credit; your pay came every four months; there was nothing to figure out or decide — you just had to avoid doing anything considered bad in the Pavlograd regiment and, when given an order, do exactly what was clearly and plainly commanded — and all would be well.

Having re-entered the fixed world of regimental life, Rostov felt the same joy and relief a tired man feels on lying down to rest. Life in the regiment during this campaign was all the pleasanter because, after his loss to Dolokhov — for which, despite all his family's consolation, he could not forgive himself — he had resolved to atone by serving not as before, but truly well, and by being a perfectly first-rate comrade and officer — in short, a splendid man altogether. This seemed so difficult out in the world, but so achievable in the regiment.
After his losses, he had resolved to repay his parents within five years. He received ten thousand rubles a year but now decided to take only two thousand and leave the rest for the debt.

The Russian army, after repeated retreats, advances, and battles at Pultusk and Preussisch-Eylau, was now concentrated near Bartenstein, awaiting the Emperor's arrival and the start of a new campaign.

The Pavlograd regiment, which belonged to the force that had served in the 1805 campaign, had been brought up to strength in Russia and arrived too late for the first engagements. It had fought neither at Pultusk nor at Preussisch-Eylau, and when it joined the army in the field during the second half of the campaign, it was attached to Platov's division.

Platov's division was operating independently of the main army. Several times units of the Pavlograd regiment had exchanged fire with the enemy, taken prisoners, and once even captured Marshal Oudinot's carriages. In April the Pavlograds had been stationed for several weeks near a completely ruined and deserted German village.

A thaw had set in — it was muddy and cold, the ice on the river was breaking up, and the roads had become impassable. For days on end, neither food for the men nor fodder for the horses had been delivered. Since no transports could get through, the men scattered through the abandoned villages searching for potatoes, but found hardly any of those either.

Everything had been eaten up and the inhabitants had fled. Those who remained were worse off than beggars, with nothing left to take. Even the soldiers — usually pitiless enough — often gave them the last of their own rations instead of taking from them.

The Pavlograd regiment had lost only two men wounded in battle but had lost nearly half its strength to hunger and disease. In the hospitals death was so certain that soldiers with fevers or the swelling caused by bad food preferred to stay on duty; they dragged their legs to the front line rather than go to the hospitals. When spring came, the soldiers found a plant just pushing through the ground that looked like asparagus. They called it "Mashka's sweet root" for some reason. It was very bitter, but they roamed the fields digging it up with their sabers and eating it, though they'd been ordered not to, since it was poisonous. That spring a new disease broke out — swelling of the arms, legs, and face — which the doctors attributed to eating this root. But despite everything, the men of Denisov's squadron ate mainly "Mashka's sweet root," because it was now the second week that the last biscuits were being rationed out at half a pound per man, and the potatoes they'd received had sprouted and frozen.
The horses had also been fed for two weeks on straw pulled from thatched roofs and had become terribly thin, though still covered with tufts of matted winter fur.

Despite this deprivation, soldiers and officers went on living as usual. Despite their pale, swollen faces and ragged uniforms, the hussars formed up for roll call, kept things in order, groomed their horses, polished their weapons, brought in roof straw instead of fodder, and gathered around the caldrons for dinner — from which they rose still hungry, joking about their wretched food and their hunger. As always, in their spare time they lit bonfires and stripped down to warm themselves by the flames, smoked, picked out and roasted sprouting rotten potatoes, and told stories of Potemkin's and Suvorov's campaigns, or tales of Alyosha the Sly or the priest's hired man Mikolka.

The officers, as usual, lived two or three to a room in roofless, half-ruined houses. The senior officers tried to gather straw and potatoes — food for the men in general. The junior officers occupied themselves as before, some playing cards (there was plenty of money, though no food), some with more innocent games like quoits and skittles. The overall course of the campaign was rarely discussed, partly because nothing definite was known, partly because there was a vague sense that things were going badly.

Rostov lived as before with Denisov, and since their furlough they had become closer than ever. Denisov never mentioned Rostov's family, but by the tender friendship his commander showed him, Rostov could tell that the older hussar's hopeless love for Natasha played a part in deepening their bond. Denisov clearly tried to keep Rostov out of danger as much as possible, and after each action he greeted his safe return with obvious joy. On one of his foraging expeditions, in a deserted, ruined village where he had come looking for food, Rostov found a family — an old Pole and his daughter with a baby in her arms. They were half-clothed, starving, too weak to walk, and had no way of getting a carriage. Rostov brought them to his quarters, put them in his own lodging, and kept them for several weeks while the old man recovered. One of his comrades, talking about women, began teasing Rostov, saying he was shrewder than any of them and that it wouldn't be a bad idea to introduce the pretty Polish girl he'd rescued. Rostov took the joke as an insult, flared up, and said such unpleasant things that Denisov could barely prevent a duel. When the officer had left, Denisov — who didn't himself know what Rostov's relationship with the Polish girl might be — began scolding him for his hot temper, and Rostov replied:
"Say what you like. She is like a sister to me, and I can't tell you how it hurt me... because... well, for that reason."
Denisov patted him on the shoulder and began rapidly pacing the room without looking at Rostov, as he always did in moments of deep feeling.
"Ah, what a crazy breed you Rostovs are!" he muttered, and Rostov noticed tears in his eyes.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: In April the troops were energized by news of the Emperor's arrival, but Rostov had no chance to attend the review at Bartenstein, as the Pavlograds were stationed at the outposts far from there.

They were bivouacking. Denisov and Rostov were living in an earth dugout that the soldiers had made for them, roofed with branches and turf. The dugout was built in the style that had become fashionable: a trench three and a half feet wide, nearly five feet deep, and eight feet long. At one end, steps were cut into the earth, forming the entrance and vestibule. The trench itself was the room, in which the lucky ones — like the squadron commander — had a plank laid on supports at the far end to serve as a table. On each side, the earth was cut back about two and a half feet, creating beds and couches. The roof was built so you could stand up in the middle and even sit up on the beds if you stayed close to the table. Denisov, who lived well because his soldiers liked him, also had a plank set into the roof at the far end with a piece of broken but mended glass for a window. When it was very cold, embers from the soldiers' campfire were placed on a bent sheet of iron on the steps in the "reception room" — as Denisov called that part of the dugout — and it became so warm that the officers, of whom there were always some visiting Denisov and Rostov, sat around in their shirtsleeves.

In April, Rostov was on orderly duty. One morning between seven and eight, returning after a sleepless night, he sent for embers, changed his rain-soaked underclothes, said his prayers, drank tea, warmed up, tidied the things on the table and in his corner, and then — his face glowing from the wind, wearing nothing but his shirt — lay on his back with his arms behind his head. He was pleasantly considering the likelihood of a promotion in a few days for his last scouting mission, and was waiting for Denisov, who had gone out somewhere and with whom he wanted to talk.
Suddenly he heard Denisov shouting behind the hut in an agitated, ringing voice. Rostov moved to the window to see who he was talking to and saw the quartermaster, Topchenko.
"I ordered you not to let them eat that Mashka root stuff!" Denisov was shouting. "And I saw with my own eyes how Lazarchuk brought some from the fields."
"I've given the order again and again, your honor, but they won't obey," answered the quartermaster.

Rostov lay back on his bed and thought contentedly: "Let him fuss and bustle — my job's done and I'm lying here. Perfect!" He could hear Lavrushka — Denisov's sly, bold orderly — talking with the quartermaster. Lavrushka was saying something about loaded wagons, biscuits, and oxen he'd seen when out looking for provisions.
Then Denisov's voice was heard shouting further and further away: "Saddle up! Second platoon!"
"Where are they off to now?" thought Rostov.

Five minutes later Denisov came into the hut, climbed with muddy boots onto the bed, lit his pipe, furiously scattered his things about, grabbed his weighted whip, buckled on his saber, and headed out again. When Rostov asked where he was going, he answered vaguely and irritably that he had some business to attend to.

"Let God and our great sovereign judge me afterward!" said Denisov as he went, and Rostov heard the hooves of several horses splashing through the mud. He didn't even bother to find out where Denisov had gone. Having gotten warm in his corner, he fell asleep and didn't leave the hut until evening. Denisov had not yet returned. The weather had cleared up, and near the next hut two officers and a cadet were playing a throwing game, laughing as their stakes buried themselves in the soft mud. Rostov joined them. In the middle of the game, the officers noticed some wagons approaching, with fifteen hussars on their gaunt horses riding behind. The wagons, escorted by the hussars, drew up at the picket ropes, and a crowd of hussars surrounded them.
"There — Denisov's been worrying," said Rostov, "and here are the provisions."
"So they are!" said the officers. "The soldiers will be thrilled!"
A little behind the hussars came Denisov, accompanied by two infantry officers with whom he was arguing.
Rostov went to meet them.
"I'm warning you, Captain," one of the officers — a short, thin man, obviously furious — was saying.
"Haven't I told you I won't give them up?" Denisov replied.
"You'll answer for this, Captain. It's mutiny — seizing your own army's transport. Our men haven't eaten in two days."
"And mine haven't eaten in two weeks," said Denisov.
"It's robbery! You'll answer for it, sir!" said the infantry officer, raising his voice.
"What are you pestering me for?" cried Denisov, suddenly losing his temper. "I'll answer for it, not you — and you'd better clear off before you get hurt. Go! Get out!" he shouted at the officers.
"Very well, then!" shouted the little officer, undaunted and not budging. "If you insist on robbing, I'll —"
"Go to the devil! Quick march, while you're still in one piece!" And Denisov turned his horse on the officer.
"Very well, very well!" muttered the officer threateningly, and turning his horse, he trotted away, bouncing in his saddle.
"A dog on a fence! A real dog on a fence!" shouted Denisov after him — the most insulting thing a cavalryman could say to a mounted infantryman — and riding up to Rostov, he burst out laughing.
"I seized those transports from the infantry by force!" he said. "After all, I can't let our men starve."

The wagons that had reached the hussars had been assigned to an infantry regiment, but when Lavrushka discovered the transport was unguarded, Denisov and his hussars had seized it by force. Biscuits were distributed freely to the soldiers, who even shared them with the other squadrons.
The next day the regimental commander sent for Denisov and, holding his fingers spread in front of his eyes, said:

"This is how I see the matter: I know nothing about it and won't open an investigation. But I advise you to ride to the staff and settle things in the commissariat department — if possible, sign a receipt for the supplies. Otherwise, since the demand was logged against an infantry regiment, there'll be trouble, and the affair could end badly."

From the regimental commander, Denisov rode straight to the staff, sincerely intending to follow this advice. That evening he returned to the dugout in a state Rostov had never seen him in before. Denisov couldn't speak — he was gasping for breath. When Rostov asked what was wrong, he could only manage some incoherent curses and threats in a hoarse, feeble voice.
Alarmed by Denisov's condition, Rostov suggested he undress, drink some water, and send for the doctor.
"Try me for robbery... oh! More water... Let them try me, but I'll always thrash scoundrels... and I'll tell the Emperor... Ice..." he muttered.
The regimental doctor, when he arrived, said bleeding was absolutely necessary. A deep saucer of black blood was drawn from Denisov's hairy arm, and only then could he tell what had happened.

"I get there," Denisov began. "'Where's your chief's office?' They pointed it out. 'Please wait.' 'I've ridden twenty miles and have duties — I can't wait. Announce me.' Very well — so out comes the chief himself, and he decides to lecture me: 'It's robbery!' 'Robbery,' I say, 'is not done by the man who seizes food to feed his soldiers, but by the man who takes it to fill his own pockets!' 'Be quiet!' 'Very well!' Then he says: 'Go give a receipt to the commissary, but your case will be referred to headquarters.' I go to the commissary. I walk in, and at the table — who do you think? No, wait! Who is it that's starving us?" shouted Denisov, slamming his fist on the table so hard it nearly broke and the glasses jumped. "Telyanin! 'What? So it's you who's been starving us? Take this! And this!' And I smashed him right in the face... 'Oh, you... you...' And I started thrashing him... Well, I had some fun, I can tell you!" cried Denisov, gleeful yet furious, his white teeth showing under his black mustache. "I'd have killed him if they hadn't dragged him away!"
"But what are you shouting for? Calm down," said Rostov. "You've opened up your arm again. Wait — let me rebandage it."
Denisov was bandaged up again and put to bed. The next day he woke up calm and cheerful.

But at noon the regimental adjutant came into Rostov and Denisov's dugout with a grave expression and regretfully showed them a document addressed to Major Denisov from the regimental commander, informing them of an inquiry into the previous day's events. The adjutant told them the affair was likely to take a very bad turn: a court-martial had been convened, and given the current severity against marauding and insubordination, demotion to the ranks would be the best Denisov could hope for.

The case, as presented by the complainants, was that Major Denisov, after seizing the transports while drunk, had gone to the chief quartermaster and without provocation called him a thief, threatened to strike him, and when led out had rushed into the office, beaten up two officials, and dislocated one's arm.

When Rostov pressed him with more questions, Denisov said with a laugh that he vaguely recalled some other fellow getting mixed up in it, but that it was all nonsense. He wasn't the least bit worried about any trial, and if those scoundrels dared come at him, he'd give them an answer they wouldn't soon forget.

Denisov talked about the whole thing with contempt, but Rostov knew him too well not to see that — while hiding it from everyone — he was genuinely afraid of the court-martial and worried about the case, which was clearly going badly. Every day brought letters of inquiry and notices from the court, and on the first of May, Denisov was ordered to hand his squadron over to the next in seniority and appear before his division's staff to explain his behavior at the commissariat office. The day before, Platov reconnoitered with two Cossack regiments and two squadrons of hussars. Denisov, as was his habit, rode out in front of the line, showing off his courage. A bullet from a French sharpshooter hit him in the fleshy part of his leg. At any other time Denisov would not have left the regiment for so minor a wound, but now he used it as an excuse to avoid the staff hearing and went to the hospital.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: In June the Battle of Friedland was fought, in which the Pavlograds took no part, and afterward an armistice was declared. Rostov, who felt his friend's absence keenly, having had no news of him since he left and being very anxious about his wound and his legal troubles, took advantage of the armistice to get leave and visit Denisov in the hospital.

The hospital was in a small Prussian town that had been devastated twice by Russian and French troops. Because it was summer, when everything is so beautiful outdoors, the little town looked especially dismal with its broken roofs and fences, its filthy streets, its ragged inhabitants, and the sick and drunken soldiers wandering about.

The hospital occupied a brick building with some of its window frames and panes broken, surrounded by a courtyard enclosed by the remnants of a wooden fence that had been torn apart. Several bandaged soldiers with pale, swollen faces were sitting or walking about in the sunshine in the yard.

The moment Rostov entered the building, he was enveloped by a smell of decay and the stale air of a hospital. On the stairs he met a Russian army doctor smoking a cigar, followed by a Russian assistant.
"I can't tear myself in half," the doctor was saying. "Come to Makar Alexeevich's this evening. I'll be there."
The assistant asked some more questions.
"Oh, do the best you can! What difference does it make?" The doctor noticed Rostov coming up the stairs.
"What do you want, sir?" said the doctor. "What do you want? The bullets spared you — are you here to catch typhus? This place is a death trap, sir."
"How so?" asked Rostov.

"Typhus, sir. Anyone who comes in here dies. Only the two of us — Makeev and I" — he pointed at the assistant — "are still standing. Five doctors have died in this place already. When a new one arrives, he's finished within a week," said the doctor with obvious pride. "Prussian doctors have been invited, but our allies don't care for it at all."
Rostov explained that he wanted to see Major Denisov of the hussars, who had been wounded.

"I have no idea — I can't tell you, sir. Just think! I'm alone in charge of three hospitals with over four hundred patients! It's a good thing the charitable Prussian ladies send us two pounds of coffee and some lint each month, or we'd be done for!" he laughed. "Four hundred, sir, and they keep sending me fresh ones. There are four hundred, aren't there?" he asked, turning to the assistant.
The assistant looked exhausted — clearly irritated and waiting for the chatty doctor to leave.
"Major Denisov," Rostov said again. "He was wounded at Molliten."
"Dead, I think. Eh, Makeev?" the doctor asked indifferently.
The assistant, however, did not confirm the doctor's words.
"Is he tall and with reddish hair?" asked the doctor.
Rostov described Denisov's appearance.
"There was one like that," said the doctor, sounding pleased. "That one's dead, I think. But I'll check our list. We had a list. Do you have it, Makeev?"
"Makar Alexeevich has the list," the assistant answered. "But if you go to the officers' ward, you'll see for yourself," he added, turning to Rostov.
"Better not, sir," said the doctor. "You might end up staying here yourself."
But Rostov politely excused himself from the doctor and asked the assistant to show him the way.
"Just don't blame me!" the doctor shouted after him.

Rostov and the assistant entered the dark corridor. The smell was so overpowering there that Rostov had to hold his nose and stop to gather himself before going on. A door opened on the right, and a gaunt, sallow man on crutches — barefoot, wearing only his underclothes — limped out and, leaning against the doorframe, stared with glittering, envious eyes at the people passing by. Glancing through the door, Rostov saw sick and wounded men lying on the floor on straw and overcoats.
"May I go in and look?"
"What's there to see?" said the assistant.

But precisely because the assistant obviously didn't want him to go in, Rostov entered the soldiers' ward. The foul air, which he'd already started getting used to in the corridor, was even stronger here — different, more acrid — and one could tell this was where it originated.

In the long room, brightly lit by sun through the large windows, the sick and wounded lay in two rows with their heads against the walls, leaving a passage down the middle. Most were unconscious and took no notice of the visitors. Those who were awake raised themselves or lifted their thin, yellow faces, all staring at Rostov with the same expression — hope, relief, reproach, and envy of someone else's health. Rostov walked to the center of the room and through the open doors saw the same scene in the two rooms beyond. He stopped and looked around in silence. He had not expected anything like this. Right in front of him, almost blocking the passage on the bare floor, lay a sick man — probably a Cossack, judging by his haircut. The man lay on his back, his massive arms and legs stretched out. His face was purple, his eyes rolled back until only the whites showed, and on his bare legs and arms — still red — the veins stood out like cords. He was knocking the back of his head against the floor, hoarsely repeating a single word over and over. Rostov listened and made it out. It was: "Drink... drink... a drink!" Rostov looked around for someone to help this man back to his place and bring him water.
"Who looks after the sick here?" he asked the assistant.
Just then a commissariat soldier — a hospital orderly — marched stiffly in from the next room and drew himself up in front of Rostov.
"Good day, your honor!" he shouted, rolling his eyes at Rostov, evidently taking him for a hospital official.
"Get this man to his place and bring him water," said Rostov, pointing to the Cossack.
"Yes, your honor," the soldier replied with gusto, rolling his eyes even more and standing even straighter — but not moving.

"No — nothing can be done here," thought Rostov, lowering his eyes. He was about to leave when he became aware of an intense gaze fixed on him from the right. He turned. Near the corner, sitting on an overcoat, was an old, unshaven, gray-bearded soldier, thin as a skeleton, with a stern sallow face and eyes locked on Rostov. The man's neighbor on one side was whispering something to him, pointing at Rostov. The old man clearly wanted to speak. Rostov moved closer and saw that the man had only one leg bent beneath him — the other had been amputated above the knee. His neighbor on the other side, who lay motionless at some distance with his head thrown back, was a young soldier with a snub nose. His pale, waxy face was still freckled, and his eyes were rolled back. Rostov looked at the young soldier and felt a cold chill run down his spine.
"Why, this one seems..." he began, turning to the assistant.
"We've been begging and begging, your honor," said the old soldier, his jaw trembling. "He's been dead since this morning. We're men after all, not dogs."
"I'll send someone right away. He'll be removed — removed immediately," said the assistant quickly. "Let's go, your honor."
"Yes, yes, let's go," said Rostov hastily, and with lowered eyes, trying to make himself invisible, he hurried between the rows of reproachful, envious eyes fixed on him, and escaped from the room.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: Having returned to the regiment and told the commander about Denisov's situation, Rostov rode to Tilsit with the letter to the Emperor.
On the thirteenth of June, the French and Russian Emperors arrived in Tilsit. Boris Drubetskoy had asked the important personage he served to include him in the suite for the Tilsit visit.
"I'd like to see the great man," he said, referring to Napoleon — whom until now he, like everyone else, had always called Buonaparte.
"You are speaking of Buonaparte?" asked the general with a smile.
